articles.title: Fatigable weakness, ptosis and diplopia
articles.th: อ่อนแรงที่แย่ลงเมื่อใช้งาน หนังตาตก เห็นภาพซ้อน — นึกถึงโรครอยต่อเส้นประสาท-กล้ามเนื้อก่อน
body: Weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest points to the neuromuscular junction. Look at the eyes first: asymmetric ptosis that drops further during sustained upgaze, variable diplopia and normal pupils make myasthenia gravis the leading diagnosis. Reflexes and sensation stay normal.

Three questions sort the mimics. Are the pupils involved? Dilated, sluggish pupils with descending paralysis suggest botulism. Are the legs and autonomic system affected more than the eyes? Think Lambert–Eaton, especially in a smoker. Is the ophthalmoplegia fixed and symmetric? Consider a mitochondrial or dystrophic myopathy, or restrictive thyroid eye disease (lid retraction rather than ptosis).

Bedside: sustained upgaze and the ice pack test. Laboratory: AChR, then MuSK/LRP4 antibodies; repetitive stimulation or single-fibre EMG; CT chest for thymoma. Monitor vital capacity whenever bulbar or neck weakness is present.

articles.title: Acute ascending or flaccid weakness
articles.th: แขนขาอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันลามขึ้น รีเฟล็กซ์หาย — นึกถึง GBS แต่ต้องแยกไขสันหลัง รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ และเกลือแร่
body: Symmetric weakness that climbs from the legs over days, with lost reflexes and mild sensory symptoms after an infection, is Guillain–Barré syndrome until shown otherwise. The danger is respiratory and autonomic failure, so serial vital capacity matters more than oxygen saturation.

Before settling on GBS, look for a sensory level and early bladder failure (spinal cord), fatigable eye signs with normal reflexes (myasthenia), descending paralysis with fixed pupils (botulism) and low potassium (periodic paralysis). Pure motor disease after diarrhoea suggests the axonal form AMAN; early nerve studies can be misleading, and repeat studies separate reversible nodal block from true demyelination.
If the illness keeps progressing beyond 8 weeks, or relapses after treatment, reconsider acute-onset CIDP or an antibody-mediated nodopathy.

articles.title: Chronic demyelinating neuropathy and CIDP mimics
articles.th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมแบบ demyelinating เรื้อรัง — แยก CIDP จากโรคที่เลียนแบบ เช่น nodopathy, anti-MAG, POEMS, MMN, CMT
body: CIDP weakens proximal and distal muscles over more than 8 weeks, with widespread areflexia and large-fibre sensory loss, and usually responds to IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange. Proximal weakness is the clue that separates it from length-dependent axonal neuropathies.

Many disorders imitate it. Ask: is there a paraprotein? IgM with anti-MAG gives a distal sensory-ataxic pattern with tremor; a lambda band with organomegaly, skin change and high VEGF means POEMS. Is the patient young with tremor, or older with nephrotic syndrome, and not responding to IVIG? Test for NF155 and contactin-1 antibodies. Is weakness asymmetric, purely motor and nerve-by-nerve? That is multifocal motor neuropathy. Lifelong, uniform slowing with pes cavus suggests Charcot–Marie–Tooth.
Every chronic demyelinating neuropathy deserves serum and urine immunofixation.

articles.title: Nodo-paranodopathies
articles.th: nodopathy คือโรคที่แอนติบอดีโจมตีบริเวณ node/paranode — คล้าย GBS/CIDP แต่รุนแรงและไม่ตอบสนอง IVIG
body: The node of Ranvier and its paranodal junctions hold the sodium channels and the glial–axonal seal that make saltatory conduction work. Antibodies against these structures produce conduction failure that can reverse quickly or progress to axon loss, which does not fit the old axonal-versus-demyelinating split.

Clinically these patients look like GBS or CIDP with atypical features: severe distal motor weakness, sensory ataxia, tremor (NF155), older age and nephrotic syndrome (contactin-1), neuropathic pain (Caspr1), or a catastrophic GBS-like illness with cranial and autonomic involvement (pan-neurofascin).

Most antibodies are IgG4, which does not activate complement — one reason IVIG often fails. Plasma exchange, steroids and especially early rituximab work better. Test for nodal antibodies when 'GBS' or 'CIDP' is unusually severe or IVIG-resistant.

articles.title: Neuropathy with a paraprotein
articles.th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอล — แยกชนิด IgM/IgG/IgA และหาโรคเม็ดเลือดที่ซ่อนอยู่
body: A monoclonal protein turns up in about one in ten people with an unexplained chronic neuropathy, and becomes commoner with age, so the link may be coincidental. The job is to decide whether the paraprotein is causing the neuropathy and whether a malignant clone lies behind it.

The pattern guides the search. IgM with a slow, distal, sensory-ataxic demyelinating neuropathy suggests anti-MAG (or Waldenström). IgG or IgA with a CIDP-like picture is treated much like CIDP. A painful small-fibre neuropathy with autonomic failure suggests AL amyloidosis. Painful mononeuritis multiplex with purpura suggests cryoglobulinaemia. A lambda band with a disabling motor neuropathy, organomegaly, skin changes and very high VEGF suggests POEMS.
Workup: immunofixation of serum and urine, free light chains, and haematology review (marrow, skeletal imaging), adding anti-MAG, VEGF, cryoglobulins or fat pad biopsy as the pattern suggests.

articles.title: Sudden focal deficit
articles.th: อาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่เกิดทันที — คิดถึง stroke ก่อน ตรวจน้ำตาลและ CT ทันที
body: A deficit that is maximal at onset and fits one arterial territory is vascular until proven otherwise. Time last known well, a glucose check and a non-contrast CT come first, because they decide reperfusion: CT separates haemorrhage from infarction, and CT angiography finds large-vessel occlusions suitable for thrombectomy.

The common mimics have tell-tale features: a witnessed seizure before the weakness (Todd's paralysis), positive spreading symptoms followed by headache (migraine aura), a low glucose (hypoglycaemia), and inconsistent weakness with a positive Hoover sign (functional disorder).
After the acute phase, the mechanism drives prevention: cardiac rhythm, carotid imaging, small vessel risk factors, and in young patients dissection or venous thrombosis.

articles.title: Thunderclap and worst-ever headache
articles.th: ปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันทีภายในนาที — ต้องหาเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองและสาเหตุอันตรายอื่นทุกครั้ง
body: A headache that reaches full intensity within a minute is a red flag regardless of how well the patient looks. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is the first concern: CT within 6 hours is very sensitive; later presentations need lumbar puncture for xanthochromia and vascular imaging.

If the CT and CSF are clear, think of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction (recurrent thunderclaps over days, triggers such as exertion or serotonergic drugs), cervical artery dissection (neck pain, Horner), cerebral venous thrombosis, and pituitary apoplexy (visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, low cortisol).

articles.title: Papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure
articles.th: จอประสาทตาบวมจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง — ต้องหาก้อน หลอดเลือดดำอุดตัน ก่อนวินิจฉัย IIH
body: Bilateral optic disc swelling with headache means raised pressure until proven otherwise. Imaging must exclude a mass and venous sinus thrombosis before a lumbar puncture measures the opening pressure.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension can only be called idiopathic after other causes are ruled out, typically in women with recent weight gain; the outcome that matters is vision, so formal visual fields guide treatment. A sixth nerve palsy can appear without any lesion in the brainstem (false localising).

articles.title: Parkinsonism: idiopathic or atypical?
articles.th: พาร์กินสันแท้หรือชนิด atypical — ดูความไม่สมมาตร การล้มเร็ว การกลอกตา ระบบอัตโนมัติ และการตอบสนองต่อเลโวโดปา
body: Bradykinesia with decrement is the required feature; rest tremor and rigidity support it. Idiopathic Parkinson's disease starts on one side, stays asymmetric and responds clearly to levodopa.

Red flags change the diagnosis. Falls in the first year and slow vertical saccades suggest PSP. Early severe autonomic failure, cerebellar signs or stridor suggest MSA. Asymmetric apraxia and cortical sensory loss suggest corticobasal degeneration. Early fluctuating cognition with visual hallucinations suggests Lewy body dementia. Symmetric signs on dopamine-blocking drugs suggest drug-induced parkinsonism, and a magnetic gait with incontinence suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.

articles.title: Tremor at the bedside
articles.th: แยกชนิดอาการสั่นจากสถานการณ์ที่เกิด: ขณะพัก ขณะยกค้าง หรือเมื่อเข้าใกล้เป้าหมาย
body: Classify tremor by when it appears. At rest, disappearing with movement: parkinsonian. With arms held out and during action, bilateral and often familial: essential tremor (check thyroid and drugs). Worsening as the finger approaches a target: cerebellar outflow, for example in multiple sclerosis. Jerky, position-specific tremor with abnormal posture: dystonic.
Tremor with neuropathy is a clue in its own right — anti-MAG and neurofascin-155 neuropathies both cause disabling action tremor.

articles.title: Cognitive decline: tempo tells the story
articles.th: สมองเสื่อม — ความเร็วของการดำเนินโรคช่วยแยกสาเหตุ หลายปี (AD) เป็นขั้น (หลอดเลือด) หรือภายในเดือน (CJD/autoimmune)
body: Years of insidious memory loss with failed cueing suggests Alzheimer's disease. Stepwise decline, slowed thinking and executive problems with white matter disease suggest vascular cognitive impairment, which often coexists with Alzheimer pathology. Early behavioural change points to frontotemporal dementia; fluctuations, hallucinations and REM sleep behaviour disorder to Lewy body dementia.

Decline over weeks to months is a different problem: look for treatable autoimmune encephalitis, infection, metabolic and nutritional causes before accepting prion disease. Lobar microbleeds in an older patient raise cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

articles.title: Acute vertigo: peripheral or central?
articles.th: เวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุน — แยกหูชั้นในกับก้านสมอง/สมองน้อยด้วยรูปแบบเวลาและการตรวจ HINTS
body: Ask about timing first. Seconds of spinning with head movement is BPPV — confirm with Dix–Hallpike and treat with repositioning. Continuous vertigo for days is an acute vestibular syndrome: vestibular neuritis or a posterior circulation stroke. Recurrent attacks of minutes to hours suggest vestibular migraine or Ménière's disease.

In the acute vestibular syndrome, HINTS helps: an abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus and no skew favour a peripheral cause; a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation demand urgent imaging for stroke.

articles.title: Spinal cord syndromes
articles.th: อาการไขสันหลัง — ขาอ่อนแรงสองข้าง ชาถึงระดับหนึ่ง ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ต้อง MRI ด่วนเพื่อหาการกดทับ
body: Weakness of both legs with a sensory level and bladder disturbance localises to the cord. The first priority is an urgent MRI of the whole spine to exclude compression from tumour, disc, abscess or haematoma.

Without compression, tempo and pattern guide the cause: hyperacute (infarction), days (inflammatory: MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, post-infectious), weeks to months with dorsal column loss and neuropathy (B12 or copper deficiency, nitrous oxide), or lightning pains with Argyll Robertson pupils (tabes dorsalis).

articles.title: Fever with headache or confusion
articles.th: ไข้ร่วมปวดศีรษะหรือสับสน — ให้ยาปฏิชีวนะและ acyclovir ก่อนรอผล ถ้าสงสัย
body: Fever, headache and neck stiffness suggest meningitis; fever with confusion, behavioural change or seizures suggests encephalitis. Do not wait for imaging or lumbar puncture to give empirical antibiotics, and add acyclovir when encephalitis is possible.

CSF patterns help: neutrophils with low glucose (bacterial), lymphocytes with very low glucose and very high protein (tuberculous or fungal), lymphocytes with normal glucose (viral or autoimmune). Subacute psychiatric change with seizures and dyskinesia in a young woman suggests anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

articles.title: Seizures, status and their mimics
articles.th: ชัก — แยกจากเป็นลมและ dissociative seizure; ชักเกิน 5 นาทีถือเป็น status ต้องรักษาทันที
body: A convulsion lasting more than five minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery, is status epilepticus: check glucose, give a benzodiazepine, then a second-line agent, and search for the cause.

For a single event, the witness account decides. Reflex syncope has a prodrome and quick recovery even if a few jerks occur. Dissociative seizures are often long, with eyes closed and fluctuating movements. Morning jerks in a teenager suggest juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; an epigastric rising sensation and automatisms suggest temporal lobe epilepsy.

articles.title: Upper versus lower motor neuron signs
articles.th: แยกรอยโรค UMN กับ LMN — ถ้าพบทั้งสองแบบในแขนขาเดียวกันโดยไม่มีอาการชา นึกถึง ALS
body: Upper motor neuron lesions give spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus, Hoffmann and Babinski signs, with weakness in a pyramidal pattern. Lower motor neuron lesions give wasting, fasciculations, low tone and reduced reflexes.

The combination matters. UMN and LMN signs together in the same region without sensory loss suggest ALS; absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars suggest combined cord and nerve disease such as B12 deficiency. Pure LMN weakness following individual nerves, with conduction block, suggests multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable mimic of ALS.

articles.title: Proximal weakness: muscle or something else?
articles.th: อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา — แยกกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อม และโรครอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ
body: Difficulty rising from a chair or lifting the arms with preserved reflexes and sensation suggests a myopathy. Weeks of symmetric weakness with a rash means dermatomyositis; an older patient with finger flexor and quadriceps weakness has inclusion body myositis; asymmetric scapular winging with facial weakness suggests FSHD; myotonia with distal weakness and cataract suggests myotonic dystrophy.

Do not forget the junction: Lambert–Eaton causes proximal leg weakness with autonomic symptoms, and myasthenia can present with neck and shoulder weakness. CK, EMG, myositis antibodies, muscle MRI and targeted genetics sort most cases.

articles.title: Young-onset progressive ataxia: recessive causes
articles.th: เดินเซที่แย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ ก่อนอายุ 30 โดยไม่มีประวัติครอบครัวแบบยีนเด่น — คิดถึง ataxia ยีนด้อย และหากลุ่มที่รักษาได้ก่อนเสมอ
body: A steadily worsening ataxia that starts before about 30, with affected siblings, parental consanguinity or no family history at all, is likely recessive once acute and acquired causes (stroke, drugs, alcohol, thiamine, autoimmune, coeliac, tumour) are out. Friedreich ataxia is the most common: areflexia, sensory loss, extensor plantars and little cerebellar atrophy early. Ataxia telangiectasia and the oculomotor apraxia ataxias come next, with head thrusts, chorea, neuropathy and a raised AFP. ARSACS adds spasticity and thick retinal fibres; POLG disease adds ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and seizures.

Hunt first for the treatable ones, because early therapy changes the outcome: AVED (vitamin E), abetalipoproteinaemia (vitamin E and a low-fat diet), cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (chenodeoxycholic acid), Refsum disease (phytanic acid diet), primary CoQ10 deficiency (CoQ10), Niemann–Pick type C (miglustat and newer drugs) and Wilson disease (copper chelation or zinc). Clues are night blindness, cataract, chronic diarrhoea, tendon lumps, anosmia, vertical gaze palsy, splenomegaly, psychiatric change or liver disease.

First-line work-up: serum vitamin E with a lipid profile and smear, cholestanol, phytanic acid, AFP, albumin and cholesterol, CK, lactate, copper and caeruloplasmin; nerve conduction studies (none, axonal or demyelinating, sensory-only or sensorimotor); and MRI looking for cerebellar atrophy, cord thinning, pontine stripes or dentate signal. Test FXN repeats early, then use a recessive-ataxia gene panel or exome/genome. Avoid valproate until POLG disease is excluded.

ward.title: Sudden word-finding trouble and a weak right hand
ward.cc: A 71-year-old retired teacher stopped mid-sentence at breakfast, could not find his words and dropped his spoon from the right hand. His wife brought him straight in.

items.q: When was he last seen normal, and did it start suddenly, gradually or in steps?
items.a: Normal while chatting at 07:10. At 07:20 he stopped mid-sentence; the deficit was at its worst from the first minute.
items.why: Onset time decides reperfusion eligibility; a deficit that is maximal at onset points to embolism.

items.q: Palpitations, a known irregular heartbeat, or a missed blood thinner?
items.a: An irregular pulse was noted at a health check last year; nothing was started.
items.why: Untreated atrial fibrillation is the commonest embolic source at this age.

items.q: Headache, vomiting or a seizure at onset?
items.why: Makes haemorrhage and Todd paralysis less likely, but only imaging excludes bleeding.

items.q: Diabetes medicines or a low sugar?
items.why: Hypoglycaemia is a quick, treatable stroke mimic.
Does not change management in the first hour.
Low yield for a sudden focal deficit.

items.a: Effortful, non-fluent speech; follows one-step commands; cannot repeat a phrase; names 2 of 6 objects.
items.why: Aphasia places the lesion in the dominant cortex and rules out a lacune.

items.q: Compare face, arm and leg power
items.a: Right lower face weak with the forehead spared; right arm 2/5; right leg 4+/5.
items.why: Face and arm worse than leg fits the lateral convexity (MCA territory).
Bedside evidence of atrial fibrillation.
Full fields argue against the inferior MCA division and the optic radiation.

items.a: Right arm reflexes slightly brisker; right plantar extensor.
items.why: Confirms an upper motor neuron lesion, although reflexes can be normal in the first hours.
Rarely changes the first-hour plan.
Unsafe and not needed for the decision.

pos: Non-fluent aphasia with poor repetition and naming
Right lower facial weakness, forehead spared
Right arm weaker than leg; right plantar extensor
Irregularly irregular pulse

pattern.why: Lower-face weakness sparing the forehead, arm weakness and an extensor plantar are corticospinal (upper motor neuron) signs; the aphasia adds the cortex.

options: Left frontal cortex and underlying white matter (superior division of the left MCA)
Left temporal lobe (inferior division of the left MCA)
loc.why: Aphasia means cortex. Non-fluent speech with poor repetition is frontal (Broca area). Face and arm worse than leg fits the lateral convexity, not the ACA. Full fields argue against the inferior division. A lacune does not cause aphasia.

tempo.why: Sudden onset that is maximal at the start is vascular, and a 'spectacular' maximal onset suggests embolism.

cat.why: Hyperacute focal deficit in an older man with atrial fibrillation: vascular until imaging says otherwise.

options.n: Cardioembolic stroke (atrial fibrillation and other cardiac sources)

options.w: No seizure was seen; post-ictal weakness follows a seizure and fades within hours.
Glucose was normal.
Aura spreads over minutes with positive symptoms and usually recovers; a sudden negative deficit at 71 is stroke.
Tumours grow over weeks; a sudden deficit happens only with bleeding into the tumour.

items: Cardioembolic stroke (atrial fibrillation and other cardiac sources)

ddx.why: All three are vascular. The irregular pulse puts embolism first, carotid disease is the other large-artery source, and bleeding must be excluded before thrombolysis.

options: Non-contrast CT brain with CT angiography now
MRI brain with gadolinium next week
next.why: Time-critical: CT excludes haemorrhage for thrombolysis and CTA finds a large-vessel occlusion for thrombectomy. Cardiac work-up follows.

ward.monk: Aphasia + face/arm > leg + extensor plantar → left frontal cortex (superior MCA). Sudden and maximal at onset + irregular pulse → cardioembolism. One lesion explains everything. Image now.
ward.monk_th: Aphasia ร่วมกับหน้าและแขนอ่อนแรงมากกว่าขา และ Babinski → left frontal cortex (superior MCA). เริ่มทันทีและหนักสุดตั้งแต่แรก ชีพจรไม่สม่ำเสมอ → cardioembolism รอยโรคเดียวอธิบายได้ทั้งหมด ส่ง CT/CTA ทันที

ward.title: Woke up with a weak left side
ward.cc: A 63-year-old taxi driver woke at 06:00 unable to lift his left arm properly and dragging his left leg. His speech is a little slurred.

items.q: When was he last seen normal, and has it changed since waking?
items.a: Normal when he went to bed at 23:00. It worsened slightly over the first 2 hours after waking and has been stable since.
items.why: Wake-up stroke: the clock starts when he was last seen well; a small step-up after onset is common in small deep infarcts.

items.q: Any numbness, visual loss, trouble understanding or finding words?
items.a: No numbness, no visual change, no language problem.
items.why: Absence of sensory and cortical features shapes the localization (pure motor).

items.q: Blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, and are medicines taken?
items.a: Hypertension for 12 years; stopped amlodipine 6 months ago. Type 2 diabetes. Smokes 20 a day.
items.why: Long-standing hypertension and diabetes are the main drivers of small vessel disease.

items.q: Neck pain or recent neck injury?
items.why: Screens for dissection.
Low yield here.
Does not change acute management.

items.q: Power in the left face, arm and leg
items.a: Left lower face weak; left arm 3/5 and left leg 3/5, equally.
items.why: Face = arm = leg is the key pattern.

items.q: Pinprick, joint position and two-point discrimination
items.why: Pure motor: no sensory fibres involved.

items.q: Language, neglect, extinction and visual fields
items.a: Normal language; no neglect or extinction; full fields.
items.why: No cortical signs, so not cortex.

items.a: Left reflexes brisk, left plantar extensor.
items.why: Confirms upper motor neuron involvement.
Fits hypertensive small vessel disease and matters for thrombolysis.
Low yield without headache.

pos: Left face, arm and leg weakness of equal degree
Left extensor plantar
Mild dysarthria
BP 196/108; hypertension, diabetes, smoking
neg: No aphasia, neglect or field defect

pattern.why: Hemiparesis with brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar is upper motor neuron.

options: Right posterior limb of the internal capsule
loc.why: Face, arm and leg equally weak with no cortical or sensory signs means a small lesion where motor fibres run tightly together: the posterior limb of the internal capsule (or the basis pontis). Cortex gives face-arm > leg plus cortical signs; the cervical cord spares the face.

tempo.why: Onset during sleep over minutes to hours: vascular.

cat.why: Acute deficit in a man with uncontrolled vascular risk factors.

options.n: Cardioembolic stroke (atrial fibrillation and other cardiac sources)
options.w: Possible but uncommon for a pure motor syndrome, and there is no cardiac clue.
No seizure history.
Wrong age and tempo: relapses evolve over days in younger people.
Would progress over weeks.

ddx.why: Small vessel occlusion is the usual cause of a pure motor capsular stroke. A deep hypertensive bleed can look identical. Branch atheromatous disease from intracranial atherosclerosis, common in Asian patients, gives larger deep infarcts that often worsen in the first days.

options: Non-contrast CT brain, then MRI with DWI and intracranial vessel imaging
next.why: Exclude haemorrhage first; DWI confirms the small deep infarct and vessel imaging looks for parent-artery stenosis.

ward.monk: Face = arm = leg with no cortical or sensory signs → pure motor lacunar syndrome → posterior limb of the internal capsule (or ventral pons). Hypertension, diabetes, smoking → small vessel disease; exclude a deep bleed.
ward.monk_th: หน้า แขน ขาอ่อนแรงเท่ากัน ไม่มี cortical sign และไม่มีชา → pure motor lacunar syndrome ที่ posterior limb of internal capsule ปัจจัยเสี่ยงความดัน เบาหวาน บุหรี่ → small vessel disease ต้องตัดเลือดออกในสมองด้วย CT ก่อน

ward.title: Vertigo, hoarseness and a numb face after a neck massage
ward.cc: A 38-year-old fitness instructor developed sudden spinning vertigo, vomiting and unsteadiness 5 hours ago. She cannot walk without help.

items.q: Neck pain or headache before the vertigo, and any neck manipulation?
items.a: Left posterior neck pain and occipital headache for 3 days, starting after a massage that twisted her neck.
items.why: Neck pain plus manipulation before a posterior-circulation event suggests vertebral artery dissection.

items.q: Hoarseness, trouble swallowing, hiccups or facial numbness?
items.a: Hoarse voice, chokes on water, constant hiccups, and the left side of her face feels strange.
items.why: Bulbar and trigeminal symptoms make this central (brainstem).

items.q: Is the vertigo only on head movement and over in seconds, or continuous?
items.why: Continuous vertigo is an acute vestibular syndrome, not positional vertigo.

items.q: Hearing loss or ringing in the ear?
items.why: New hearing loss with vertigo can be AICA ischaemia or labyrinthitis.
Low yield for this picture.
Not relevant here.

items.q: Pain and temperature on the face and limbs
items.a: Reduced pinprick and cold on the left face and on the right arm, trunk and leg.
items.why: Crossed sensory loss is the signature of a lateral medullary lesion.

items.a: Smaller left pupil with 1–2 mm left ptosis.
items.why: Ipsilateral Horner from the descending sympathetic tract.

items.a: Head impulse normal both ways; nystagmus changes direction with gaze; small vertical skew.
items.why: A normal head impulse during acute continuous vertigo is a central warning sign.

items.a: Left limb ataxia; cannot stand without support and falls to the left.
items.why: Ipsilateral ataxia from the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

items.a: Palate pulls to the right on 'ah'; weak voice.
items.why: Left nucleus ambiguus (IX, X).
Spared pyramid: the lesion is lateral, not medial.

pos: Crossed pain–temperature loss: left face, right body
Left Horner syndrome
Hoarseness, dysphagia, hiccups; palate weak on the left
Left limb ataxia, falls to the left
Central HINTS (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew)

pattern.why: The complaint is vertigo and imbalance, not limb weakness; the bulbar palsy is a cranial-nerve nucleus sign that helps localize.

loc.why: Ipsilateral face pain–temperature (spinal trigeminal nucleus), contralateral body (spinothalamic), ipsilateral Horner, ipsilateral palate (nucleus ambiguus) and ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle) all meet in the left lateral medulla. A normal head impulse excludes a peripheral cause.

cat.why: Sudden brainstem syndrome; in a young adult with neck pain think arterial dissection.

options.w: Peripheral: abnormal head impulse, no crossed sensory loss, Horner or bulbar signs.
Brainstem relapses evolve over days and lack the neck-pain story.
Usually hypertensive and older, with headache; no crossed sensory loss.

ddx.why: Vertebral dissection leads in a young adult with neck pain after manipulation. Paradoxical embolism through a PFO is the other young-stroke cause. Atherosclerosis is less likely without risk factors.

options: MRI brain with DWI plus CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels
next.why: Early CT is often normal in the posterior fossa; DWI shows the infarct and angiography shows the dissection.

ward.monk: Crossed face/body pain–temperature loss + ipsilateral Horner + bulbar palsy + ataxia = lateral medulla. Normal head impulse in acute vertigo is a red flag. Young + neck pain after neck twisting → vertebral dissection.
ward.monk_th: ชาเจ็บร้อนเย็นแบบไขว้ หน้าซ้าย-ตัวขวา + Horner ซ้าย + กลืนลำบากเสียงแหบ + เซซ้าย = lateral medulla ซ้าย อาการเวียนเฉียบพลันแต่ head impulse ปกติ = central คนอายุน้อยปวดคอหลังบิดคอ → vertebral artery dissection

ward.title: Double vision on looking right
ward.cc: A 27-year-old accountant has had double vision for 4 days, only when she looks to the right.

items.q: Any earlier neurological symptoms that recovered on their own?
items.a: Two years ago her right eye was blurred and painful to move for 3 weeks, then recovered fully. She was told it was eye inflammation.
items.why: A previous episode in a different place with full recovery is dissemination in time and space.

items.q: Are symptoms worse with heat or exercise?
items.a: Her legs tingle after a hot shower and settle when she cools down.
items.why: Uhthoff phenomenon supports demyelination.

items.q: Electric shocks down the back on bending the neck?
items.why: Lhermitte sign points to a cervical cord lesion.
An infection can cause a pseudorelapse or ADEM.
Raised pressure can cause a false-localizing sixth nerve palsy.
Low yield.

items.q: Eye movements on lateral gaze, watching each eye, plus convergence
items.a: On right gaze the left eye does not adduct and the right eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is intact.
items.why: Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

items.q: Acuity, colour vision, pupils and discs
items.a: Right eye 6/9, red looks washed out, right relative afferent pupillary defect, pale temporal right disc.
items.why: Evidence of an old right optic neuritis.

items.a: Brisk leg reflexes; right plantar extensor.
items.why: A third site: corticospinal tract.

items.q: Vibration and joint position in the feet
items.a: Vibration slightly reduced at the toes.
items.why: Possible dorsal column involvement.
Low yield.
Low yield here.

pos: Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Old right optic neuropathy (RAPD, temporal pallor)
Brisk leg reflexes, right extensor plantar
Uhthoff phenomenon; Lhermitte sign
Previous episode with full recovery

options: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus (dorsomedial pons or midbrain)
loc.why: An INO is named after the eye that fails to adduct, and the lesion is in the MLF on that side. Intact convergence excludes a medial rectus or third nerve problem. Here one lesion does not explain everything: the optic nerve and corticospinal signs are other sites.

tempo.why: Two episodes in different places, the first recovering to baseline: relapsing–remitting, the signature of demyelination.

cat.why: Young woman, several sites at different times, Uhthoff and Lhermitte.

options.w: Can mimic an INO, but there is no fatigability or ptosis and there are CNS signs.
Wrong age and course; a single stroke would not explain the old optic neuritis.
A mimic to consider if there are systemic features or atypical MRI findings.

ddx.why: MS is most likely: INO, mild optic neuritis with good recovery and a cord sign. NMOSD and MOGAD also cause optic neuritis and brainstem attacks; severe optic neuritis, area postrema symptoms or long cord lesions would move them up.

options: MRI brain and spinal cord with gadolinium, then CSF oligoclonal bands
next.why: MRI shows dissemination in space and time (McDonald criteria); CSF bands support it. Test AQP4 and MOG antibodies when features are atypical.

ward.monk: INO = MLF. Add old optic neuritis and UMN signs → three sites at two times: one lesion cannot explain it → dissemination in space and time → demyelinating. Relapse with recovery to baseline is the tempo clue.

ward.cc: A 56-year-old market vendor has had 6 weeks of rapidly worsening unsteadiness, slurred speech and double vision. She now needs a wheelchair.

items.a: It began 6 weeks ago; by week 3 she needed a stick; now a wheelchair.

items.a: Lost 5 kg. She felt a hard lump in her left breast 3 months ago but did not see a doctor.
items.why: A hidden cancer is the key clue for a paraneoplastic syndrome.

items.q: Alcohol, antiseizure drugs or other medicines?
items.a: No alcohol; no phenytoin, carbamazepine or lithium.
items.why: Excludes common toxic cerebellar causes.

items.q: Memory loss, sudden jerks or behaviour change?
items.why: Screens for prion disease.
Inherited ataxias are slower, but ask.
Low yield.

items.a: Wide-based gait, cannot walk heel-to-toe; ataxia of all four limbs.
items.why: Pancerebellar involvement.

items.a: Scanning dysarthria; downbeat nystagmus; jerky pursuit.
items.why: Midline and vestibulocerebellar involvement.

items.why: Finds the likely cancer.

items.a: Joint position normal; she is just as unsteady with eyes open.
items.why: Cerebellar, not sensory, ataxia.
No pyramidal or peripheral involvement.
Low yield.

pos: Subacute pancerebellar syndrome: gait, limbs, speech, downbeat nystagmus
Left breast mass with an axillary node
Weight loss 5 kg

pattern.why: Power, tone and reflexes are normal; the problem is coordination (cerebellar).

options: Dorsal columns or dorsal root ganglia (sensory ataxia)
loc.why: Gait, limb, speech and eye-movement ataxia on both sides with normal joint position sense means a symmetric cerebellar problem, not sensory ataxia.

cat.why: A subacute pancerebellar syndrome with a breast mass is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise.

options.w: No alcohol; it mainly affects gait and legs.
Progress over years with a family history.
Slower, with autonomic failure or parkinsonism.

ddx.why: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) with breast or ovarian cancer is the classic match. GAD65 ataxia is the non-paraneoplastic immune alternative. Ataxic-onset CJD also runs over weeks, so keep it on the list.

options: Paraneoplastic antibody panel in serum and CSF, plus mammography and biopsy of the breast mass
next.why: Finding and treating the cancer is the main treatment. MRI is often normal early.

ward.monk: Subacute (weeks) pancerebellar syndrome in an adult → think immune, paraneoplastic and prion before degenerative. Look for the cancer: here a breast lump. Anti-Yo (PCA-1) → breast or ovary.

watch.title: Tenecteplase before thrombectomy did not help basilar occlusion at 4.5–24 hours
watch.what: ATTENTION LATE (330 patients, China): adding tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg before thrombectomy for moderate–severe basilar artery occlusion presenting 4.5–24 hours after onset gave the same rate of functional independence at 90 days as thrombectomy alone (30% vs 30%), with similar symptomatic haemorrhage and mortality.
watch.why: In late-window basilar occlusion taken directly to a thrombectomy centre, go straight to thrombectomy; late bridging lysis adds no benefit.

watch.title: Antibody-oligonucleotide conjugate raises dystrophin in exon 44-skippable Duchenne
watch.what: EXPLORE44 (phase 1/2, 26 boys and young men): delpacibart zotadirsen increased exon 44 skipping and dystrophin and lowered muscle-damage markers with acceptable safety; phase 3 is planned. Separately, a cross-trial comparison suggested vamorolone matches prednisone and deflazacort for motor function with fewer growth effects.
watch.why: Muscle-targeted delivery may make exon skipping far more effective; watch phase 3.

watch.title: Fixing asymptomatic carotid stenosis does not improve cognition
watch.what: CREST-2 cognitive results and the CREST-H substudy: stenting or endarterectomy plus intensive medical management did not improve cognition over up to 4 years compared with intensive medical management alone, even in patients with impaired hemispheric perfusion.
watch.why: Cognitive decline is not an indication for revascularizing an asymptomatic stenosis.

watch.title: Tirofiban did not prevent worsening in branch atheromatous disease
watch.what: STRATEGY (970 patients): intravenous tirofiban plus aspirin did not reduce early neurological deterioration within 7 days or new stroke by 90 days compared with aspirin alone in stroke from branch atheromatous disease (17.1% vs 19.6%), and bleeding was rare in both groups.
watch.why: No proven way yet to stop the progressive course of branch atheromatous (deep perforator) infarcts.

watch.title: EAN/ESCMID guideline on infectious encephalitis in adults
watch.what: Two GRADE recommendations: start intravenous aciclovir as soon as encephalitis is suspected, and do not replace pathogen-specific CSF PCR with multiplex PCR panels. No recommendation for or against steroids in proven HSV encephalitis; 13 good-practice statements cover suspicion, tests and rehabilitation.
watch.why: Multiplex panels can miss HSV; send specific HSV PCR.

watch.title: Negative trials: oral tau drug in Alzheimer disease and RIPK1 inhibitor in ALS
watch.what: Ceperognastat, an oral tau-targeting drug, did not slow early symptomatic Alzheimer disease over 100 weeks. The RIPK1 inhibitor SAR443820 did not slow ALS over 24 weeks (HIMALAYA) and raised liver enzymes; development stopped.
watch.why: Two mechanisms set aside; anti-amyloid antibodies remain the only disease-modifying option in early AD.

watch.title: Orexin-2 receptor agonists work in narcolepsy type 1
watch.what: Two phase 3 trials of oveporexton (12 weeks) improved wakefulness, sleepiness and cataplexy in narcolepsy type 1; the main adverse effects were passing urine more often and short-lived trouble sleeping. A phase 2 trial of another oral agonist, alixorexton, showed large gains in maintenance-of-wakefulness latency at 6 weeks.
watch.why: These drugs act on the orexin pathway that is lost in narcolepsy type 1; likely to change first-line care once approved.

watch.title: Another negative thrombectomy trial for medium and distal vessel occlusion
watch.what: DISCOUNT (244 patients, median NIHSS 8): thrombectomy for medium or distal vessel occlusion did not improve good outcome at 3 months (62% vs 68% with medical care alone), and symptomatic haemorrhage was more frequent after thrombectomy.
watch.why: Adds to earlier neutral MeVO trials: medical treatment remains the default for most medium and distal occlusions outside trials.

watch.title: Gefurulimab: weekly self-injected complement inhibitor for AChR-positive myasthenia
watch.what: PREVAIL (260 patients, phase 3): once-weekly subcutaneous gefurulimab improved MG-ADL and QMG at 26 weeks versus placebo in AChR-antibody-positive generalized myasthenia, with benefit from week 1 and good tolerability.
watch.why: Adds a self-administered C5 option to the growing complement and FcRn toolbox.

watch.title: AAN/AHS 2026 guideline on preventive drugs for migraine
watch.what: Updated recommendations on when to start prevention and how to choose a drug, with advice for fibromyalgia, obesity, hypertension, older adults, pregnancy and lactation, sex-related factors and medication overuse, plus how to judge benefit and when to stop. A head-to-head trial (TEMPLE) found atogepant better tolerated and more effective than topiramate over 24 weeks.
watch.why: Gepants and CGRP drugs now sit alongside older oral preventives in formal guidance.

watch.title: Anticoagulation helped atrial fibrillation at intermediate stroke risk
watch.what: SINGLE-AF (South Korea): in atrial fibrillation with intermediate stroke risk, a DOAC reduced the combined rate of stroke, embolism elsewhere in the body, serious bleeding or cardiac death over 2 years, compared with leaving them untreated.
watch.why: Supports offering a DOAC at intermediate stroke risk, a group where guidance has been weak; guidelines may move.

watch.title: New gene–disease links: SCA27B phenotype widens; CACNB1 congenital myopathy; adult CLN8 vacuolar myopathy
watch.what: A SCA27B cohort describes movement-disorder features and cognitive impairment, with a third of patients first misdiagnosed as TIA because of episodic attacks. Recessive CACNB1 variants are reported as a new cause of congenital myopathy (excitation–contraction coupling), and biallelic CLN8 variants as the cause of a vacuolar myopathy beginning in adult life.
watch.why: Episodic ataxia spells in older adults can be SCA27B, not TIA; two new genes for myopathy panels.

watch.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and NAION: consensus advice
watch.what: NANOS and the AAO judge the evidence (mostly retrospective) as showing at most a small possible rise in NAION risk with semaglutide-type drugs, with a low absolute risk; decisions to start, continue or stop should be shared with the patient.
watch.why: Ask about GLP-1 agonists in every new NAION.

watch.title: ESO update: blood pressure targets after ischaemic stroke and brain haemorrhage
watch.what: Advises against routine pre-hospital BP lowering; keep BP below 185/110 before lysis and below 180/105 for 24 hours after lysis or thrombectomy; recommends against pushing systolic BP below 140 in the first 24 hours after successful thrombectomy (high certainty). watch.title: Consensus definition of MELAS

watch.title: A higher nusinersen dose for SMA

watch.title: AHA/ASA 2026 guideline for early management of acute ischaemic stroke

meq.title: A teacher whose vision clouded over in both eyes

src.label: Fineberg et al., Neurology 2026 — Resident & Fellow Clinical Reasoning

compare: Optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica (NMO-ON)
meq.stem: A 31-year-old woman who teaches at a primary school in Nonthaburi comes to the emergency room of a tertiary neurology institute in Bangkok. For five days she has had a dull headache that keeps getting worse, an ache behind both eyes that sharpens when she looks to the side, and vision that has turned cloudy in both eyes; today she cannot read the wall clock across the room. About ten days ago she had three days of fever, sore throat and heavy tiredness that settled with paracetamol. She takes no regular medicines, has never had a neurological episode before and is otherwise well.

steps.label: Initial approach
steps.q: What should you establish first in the history and bedside examination, and what is your problem list?
steps.key: Prove that the visual loss comes from the optic nerves rather than the eye media, retina or brain: best-corrected acuity in each eye, colour vision (Ishihara plates), pupils for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), confrontation fields, and fundoscopy for disc swelling, haemorrhage or exudate. Ask about pain on eye movement, tempo, infection clues (fever, rash, sexual risk, TB contact, cat scratch), earlier neurological events that suggest MS or NMOSD (myelitis, intractable hiccups or vomiting) and toxins or drugs (ethambutol, methanol). Check temperature and the rest of the neurological examination. Problem list: (1) subacute bilateral painful visual loss; (2) headache; (3) a febrile viral-type illness 10 days earlier.
steps.short: Acuity, colour, RAPD, fields, fundi; eye-movement pain; infection and demyelination history; problem = subacute bilateral painful visual loss after a febrile illness.

steps.why: Before you name a disease, prove where the visual loss comes from. Low acuity with worse colour vision and an afferent pupil defect is the signature of the optic nerve, and the fundus shows whether the front of the nerve is swollen. Hold on to the febrile illness of ten days ago; it is a clue, not background noise.

steps.label: Localization
steps.info: Best-corrected acuity is 6/36 right and 3/60 left. She reads 4 of 17 Ishihara plates with the right eye and none with the left. There is a small left RAPD. Confrontation suggests a central scotoma in each eye. Both optic discs are mildly swollen without haemorrhage or exudate; the maculae look normal and the slit lamp shows no vitreous cells. Eye movements are full but uncomfortable. The rest of the neurological examination is normal.
steps.q: Where is the lesion? Give your reasoning.
steps.key: Both optic nerves, the anterior (intraorbital) segments, left worse than right: a bilateral optic neuropathy with mild papillitis. Reduced acuity with disproportionate colour loss, central scotomas and an RAPD on the worse side mark optic nerve disease rather than retinal or media disease; pain on eye movement reflects inflamed nerve sheath near the muscle origins at the orbital apex. A chiasmal lesion would give a bitemporal pattern, and a normal macula without a star lowers neuroretinitis. Simultaneous bilateral involvement is itself atypical for MS-related optic neuritis.
steps.short: Bilateral anterior optic nerves (papillitis), left > right; not chiasm, not retina; bilaterality is atypical.

steps.why: An RAPD can still appear in bilateral disease when one nerve is worse, so a small left RAPD here means 'both nerves, the left more'. Disc swelling tells you the inflammation reaches the nerve head, and a normal macula keeps neuroretinitis lower. As soon as both eyes are involved together, switch on your 'atypical optic neuritis' alarm.

steps.label: Tempo, pattern and etiological category
steps.info: Vision kept worsening over the five days and has not yet started to recover. She has never had numbness, weakness, bladder trouble, prolonged vomiting or hiccups. Temperature 37.4 °C. No rash, no enlarged lymph nodes; the liver edge is just palpable.
steps.q: Describe the tempo and pattern, and name the most likely etiological categories.
steps.key: Subacute (over days) bilateral painful optic neuritis in a young adult, beginning about 1–2 weeks after a febrile systemic illness, with no earlier neurological events. Days with pain fit inflammation, not ischaemia (sudden, painless) or compression, toxins or LHON (slow or sequential, painless). Leading categories: (1) inflammatory — a para-infectious or post-infectious immune optic neuritis, and antibody-mediated demyelination (MOG, AQP4), which can also follow infection; (2) infective — direct infection of the nerve (syphilis, TB, viruses, Bartonella). MS-related, toxic-nutritional and hereditary causes are less likely.
steps.short: Subacute bilateral painful ON 1–2 weeks after fever → para-/post-infectious inflammatory vs direct infective vs MOG/AQP4.

steps.why: Tempo is the cheapest test you have: sudden and painless suggests a vascular cause, months of decline suggests compression or toxins, and days with pain suggests inflammation. One to two weeks after a fever is the classic window for an immune reaction set off by an infection. Keep direct infection in view as well, because steroids alone could harm such a patient.

steps.label: Differential diagnosis
steps.info: Review of systems is otherwise negative: no joint pain, mouth ulcers, cough, cat contact or recent vaccination.
steps.q: Give a ranked differential diagnosis of 4 diseases, each with one discriminating feature.
steps.key: 1. Para-/post-infectious optic neuritis — bilateral, follows a viral prodrome, may carry systemic clues (raised liver enzymes, lymphocytosis); antibody tests negative. 2. MOG-associated optic neuritis — often bilateral with marked disc swelling and long anterior nerve enhancement, frequently after infection; MOG-IgG positive. 3. AQP4-positive NMOSD optic neuritis — severe loss, long posterior or chiasmal enhancement, past myelitis or area postrema syndrome; AQP4-IgG positive. 4. Direct infectious optic neuritis (syphilis, TB, Bartonella neuroretinitis) — vitreous cells, retinal exudate or a macular star, positive serology. MS-associated optic neuritis is less likely: usually one eye, a short nerve segment and white-matter lesions on MRI.
steps.short: 1 para-infectious ON; 2 MOG-ON; 3 AQP4-NMOSD ON; 4 direct infectious ON; MS-ON less likely.

steps.why: Rank each disease by how well it explains bilateral swollen discs after a febrile illness. MOG disease is the great look-alike here because it also favours post-infectious, bilateral, swollen-disc presentations, so test for it before you settle on 'para-infectious'. The feature you list for each is exactly what you will look for in the results.

steps.label: Investigations (tertiary centre)
steps.info: She is admitted to the neurology ward of the institute; MRI, a full laboratory and an ophthalmology service are available.
steps.q: Which investigations would you order at a tertiary centre, and why?
tests: MRI orbits and brain with contrast
steps.key: MRI brain and orbits with gadolinium and fat suppression: length and site of nerve enhancement (long anterior suggests MOG, posterior or chiasmal suggests AQP4), brain or cord lesions for MS or ADEM, sheath or meningeal enhancement for infection. Serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay, because they change treatment and prognosis. LP: cells, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, and infection studies as indicated. Infection screen before or with steroids: RPR with TPHA, HIV test, chest X-ray (TB, sarcoid), and CMV and EBV serology given the prodrome. Complete blood count and liver function tests (systemic viral illness, steroid baseline). Formal perimetry and OCT as a baseline for follow-up.
steps.short: MRI orbits+brain with contrast; AQP4/MOG-IgG (CBA); LP with OCB; RPR/TPHA, HIV, CXR, CMV/EBV serology; CBC, LFT; perimetry, OCT.

points.c: MRI orbits and brain with contrast

steps.why: Each test should answer a question you raised in the differential. MRI and the two antibody tests separate MOG, NMOSD and MS, while the infection screen protects you from giving steroids to an untreated infection. The febrile prodrome is your reason to look for a systemic virus and to check the liver.

steps.label: Investigations (limited-resource hospital)
steps.info: Suppose instead she had come to a rural community hospital: CT, routine blood tests, VDRL and anti-HIV, chest X-ray and basic CSF tests are available; there is no MRI, no antibody testing and no ophthalmologist on site.
steps.q: What would you do at this hospital, what would you send out or refer for, and how can you still reach the diagnosis?
tests: CT brain and orbits with contrast
steps.key: Record Snellen acuity, Ishihara plates, RAPD, confrontation fields and direct fundoscopy as a baseline. CT brain and orbits with contrast to exclude a compressive lesion or sinus disease (it shows nerve inflammation poorly). CBC, liver tests, glucose, VDRL/RPR with TPHA, anti-HIV and chest X-ray screen for the infections that would change treatment. Basic CSF (cells, protein, glucose, opening pressure) once CT is safe. Freeze serum before steroids and send it to a reference laboratory for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG. Refer the same day to a provincial or tertiary centre for MRI and ophthalmology: severe bilateral loss should not wait. A typical picture with a negative syphilis/HIV screen, normal CT and CSF and clues of a systemic virus is enough to begin treatment after discussion with the referral centre.
steps.short: Bedside VA/colour/RAPD/fundi; CT with contrast; CBC, LFT, VDRL+TPHA, anti-HIV, CXR; basic CSF; freeze serum for AQP4/MOG; same-day referral.

points.c: CT with contrast to exclude compression
Urgent referral for MRI and eye care

steps.why: Without MRI you can still rule in the treatable infections and rule out compression, and that is most of the safety work. A frozen serum sample taken before steroids keeps the antibody question open. Severe loss in both eyes is a reason to refer today, not next week.

steps.label: Results and final diagnosis
steps.info: MRI brain and orbits with contrast: normal. CSF: 2 cells/µL, protein 0.32 g/L, normal glucose, no oligoclonal bands. AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG (cell-based): negative. RPR and TPHA non-reactive, anti-HIV negative, chest X-ray clear. ALT 168 U/L, AST 121 U/L, bilirubin normal. CMV IgG raised at a high titre; EBV serology negative. Mild lymphocytosis on CBC.
steps.q: What is the final diagnosis, and what is the mechanism in one line?
steps.key: Para-infectious (post-infectious) bilateral optic neuritis in an immunocompetent adult, most likely linked to a recent systemic CMV-type infection (high CMV IgG with a mild hepatitis). Mechanism: an immune response triggered by the infection inflames both optic nerves (molecular mimicry or bystander activation) rather than the virus destroying the nerve directly. Normal MRI and CSF, negative AQP4/MOG antibodies and a negative syphilis/HIV screen exclude the main alternatives. A high IgG alone does not date an infection; IgM, IgG avidity or CMV PCR show whether it is recent.
steps.short: Para-infectious bilateral ON after a CMV-type systemic infection; immune-mediated; antibody and infection screens negative.

steps.why: The diagnosis stands on two legs: positive signs of a systemic virus (raised liver enzymes, high CMV antibody) and negative tests for the diseases that would change long-term care. Be modest about serology: IgG records past contact, so call the CMV link 'probable' unless IgM, avidity or PCR show a recent infection.

steps.label: Specific treatment
steps.info: Her ALT is falling on repeat testing and she is afebrile, but left-eye vision has dropped to counting fingers.
steps.q: What specific treatment would you give? (No Thai national guideline for optic neuritis is known; answer according to international practice based on the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial.)
steps.basis: International standard practice based on the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) and expert consensus for atypical optic neuritis; no Thai national guideline is known (verify).
steps.key: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days (the ONTT used 250 mg every 6 hours for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for about 11 days and a short taper. Steroids speed recovery and are reasonable here because she is immunocompetent, the viral illness is resolving and the syphilis, HIV and TB screen is negative. Antivirals (ganciclovir, valganciclovir) are not routinely needed for CMV in an immunocompetent host; keep them for direct viral nerve infection or immunosuppression. If severe bilateral loss does not respond, consider plasma exchange (5–7 exchanges).
steps.short: IVMP 1 g/day × 3–5 days then oral taper after the infection screen; no routine antiviral; plasma exchange if steroid-refractory.

steps.why: In typical optic neuritis steroids change the final vision little but hasten recovery, and in severe loss of both eyes that matters for daily life. The safety step is the infection screen first, because steroids alone can worsen syphilis or TB. Keep plasma exchange in reserve for vision that does not respond.

steps.label: Supportive treatment and complications to monitor
steps.info: After three days of IV steroids the headache and eye pain settle; acuity improves to 6/18 right and 6/24 left.
steps.q: What supportive care would you give, and which complications would you monitor?
steps.key: Supportive: proton-pump inhibitor, glucose and blood pressure checks, help with steroid insomnia or agitation, analgesia, and low-vision safety advice at home. Monitor: steroid adverse effects (hyperglycaemia, hypertension, gastritis, mood change); liver enzymes until normal; acuity, colour and fields to confirm recovery and to detect relapse during the taper — relapse on withdrawal suggests MOG disease and calls for a repeat MOG test; new neurological symptoms such as myelitis or encephalopathy (ADEM). Repeat OCT and perimetry at follow-up to document residual damage.
steps.short: PPI, glucose/BP, sleep; monitor steroid effects, LFT, vision on taper (relapse → retest MOG), new neuro signs; OCT/fields later.

steps.why: In this phase most harm comes from the treatment, so plan for the steroid side effects. The disease's own warning is a relapse when steroids are withdrawn; that pattern should make you doubt the 'single post-infectious event' label and test for MOG again.

steps.label: Counselling
steps.info: She goes home on the oral taper. At 4 weeks acuity is 6/9 in both eyes and colour vision has almost returned.
steps.q: How would you counsel her and her family?
steps.key: Prognosis is usually good: most para-infectious optic neuritis recovers well over weeks to months, though colours may stay slightly dull; recurrence is uncommon while antibodies remain negative. It is not contagious once the viral illness has passed and is not inherited. Return urgently for new or worse visual loss in either eye, returning eye pain, limb weakness or numbness, bladder trouble, intractable vomiting or hiccups, or confusion. Follow-up with neuro-ophthalmology at 2–4 weeks and 3 months (acuity, fields, OCT) and repeat liver tests. Work: adjust teaching duties until reading vision returns; do not drive until acuity meets the licensing standard. Pregnancy: no restriction from the optic neuritis, but discuss timing with her obstetrician because a recent primary CMV infection carries fetal risk.
steps.short: Good recovery, low relapse; not inherited or contagious; return for new visual or neuro symptoms; OCT/fields follow-up; no driving until vision meets standard; discuss CMV before pregnancy.

steps.why: Patients remember the first sentence, so lead with the fact that recovery is the usual course. Then give concrete reasons to return, because a relapse is the signal to revisit the diagnosis. For a young woman, linking the recent CMV infection to any pregnancy plan is a thoughtful extra.

meq.monk: A young adult has days of headache, pain behind both eyes and fogging vision about ten days after a feverish illness. Low acuity, poor colour vision, central scotomas and an asymmetric RAPD place the lesion in both optic nerves, and mild disc swelling shows the front of the nerves is involved. Bilateral, simultaneous onset after a fever is atypical for MS and points to a para-infectious immune process, but MOG and AQP4 disease and direct infection (syphilis, TB) must be excluded because they change treatment. Normal MRI and CSF, negative AQP4/MOG antibodies and a negative infection screen, together with raised liver enzymes and a high CMV antibody titre, support para-infectious optic neuritis after a systemic CMV-type infection. With infection excluded, IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery; watch for steroid side effects and for relapse on the taper, which would reopen the MOG question.

meq.title: A man with a painless blur in both eyes

src.label: Diaz Curbelo et al., Neurology 2026 — Resident & Fellow Clinical Reasoning

meq.stem: A 49-year-old man who sells clothes at a night market in Chonburi attends the eye and neurology clinic of a regional hospital. Over about a week his vision has blurred in both eyes, the right more than the left, and it keeps getting worse. He has no eye pain, has not noticed red eyes and has no headache. Around two months ago a widespread, faintly itchy rash appeared over his trunk and limbs; it never touched his face and faded without treatment. He has no known medical illnesses and takes no regular medicines.

steps.label: Initial approach
steps.q: What would you ask and examine first, and what is your problem list?
steps.key: Eyes: acuity, colour vision, pupils (RAPD), fields, slit-lamp examination for anterior-chamber cells and flare, and dilated fundoscopy for disc swelling, haemorrhage or retinitis. History: sexual history, partners, earlier sexually transmitted infections and HIV risk; any genital or oral sore; the rash in detail (palms and soles, timing), hair loss, fever, lymph nodes; TB contact, cat contact, tick exposure or travel; mouth ulcers, joint or skin disease (Behçet, sarcoid); headache, tinnitus or hearing loss (VKH, otosyphilis); transient visual obscurations (raised intracranial pressure). Problem list: (1) subacute painless bilateral visual loss; (2) a preceding generalised rash that spared the face; (3) eye findings still to be defined.
steps.short: Full eye exam incl. slit lamp and dilated fundus; sexual/STI/HIV history; rash details (palms, soles, sores); problem = painless bilateral visual loss after a rash.

kw: ขยายม่านตา
เพศสัมพันธ์
แผลที่อวัยวะเพศ

steps.why: A painless blur in both eyes after a body-wide rash should make you think of a systemic illness that touches skin and eye. Examine the front of the eye as well as the back, because uveitis changes the whole differential. Ask the sexual history plainly and kindly: it is a medical question, and here the answer is decisive.

steps.label: Localization
steps.info: Acuity 6/60 right, 6/18 left; colour vision reduced on the right; mild right RAPD. Slit lamp: fine cells and flare in the anterior chamber of both eyes. Fundi: both optic discs swollen, with scattered intraretinal and peripapillary nerve-fibre-layer haemorrhages; no macular star. Fields: enlarged blind spots and generalised constriction on the right. The rest of the neurological examination is normal; no neck stiffness; hearing normal to whispered voice.
steps.q: Where are the lesions? Explain.
steps.key: Several ocular structures are inflamed: both optic nerve heads (bilateral optic neuropathy with disc oedema — papillitis or perineuritis), the anterior uvea (anterior uveitis) and the retina (haemorrhages). Optic nerve dysfunction is shown by low acuity, colour loss and an RAPD on the worse side; cells in the anterior chamber show the eye itself is inflamed. Because central vision, colour and the pupil are affected, this is not simple papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure, in which central vision is usually kept early. Uveitis plus disc swelling points to a systemic inflammatory or infectious process involving the whole eye.
steps.short: Both optic nerve heads + anterior uvea + retina; not papilloedema because acuity, colour and pupil are affected.

kw: ขั้วประสาทตา
เส้นประสาทตา
ม่านตาอักเสบ
จอประสาทตา
ความดันในกะโหลก

steps.why: Disc swelling is a sign, not a diagnosis. Papilloedema from raised pressure usually spares central vision at first, whereas here acuity, colour and the pupil are all affected, so the nerve itself is inflamed. Add cells in the anterior chamber and you are looking at an inflamed eye, which turns you toward systemic infection or granulomatous disease.

steps.label: Tempo, pattern and etiological category
steps.info: He reports unprotected sex with several partners over the past year. About four months ago he had a painless sore on the penis that healed on its own. The rash had included his palms and soles. No fever now, no tick bites, no travel abroad, no cough, no current oral or genital ulcers, no joint pain.
steps.q: What is the tempo and pattern, and which etiological category is most likely?
steps.key: Subacute (about a week) painless bilateral optic neuropathy with anterior uveitis and retinal haemorrhages, two months after a generalised rash that involved the palms and soles but spared the face, itself preceded by a painless genital sore. The sequence of a systemic illness with skin and then eye involvement fits the infective category: secondary (early) syphilis reaching the eye — ocular syphilis, which counts as early neurosyphilis. Other categories to keep: inflammatory granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, VKH) and other infections (TB, Lyme, Bartonella, viral retinitis in HIV).
steps.short: Subacute painless bilateral optic neuropathy + uveitis after a painless chancre and palm/sole rash → infective: secondary syphilis with eye involvement.

kw: กึ่งเฉียบพลัน

steps.why: The time line tells the story: a painless sore, a palm-and-sole rash weeks later, then inflammation of the eye — the natural course of syphilis in the right order. Syphilis is called the great imitator, but when the sequence is this clear it imitates nothing. Still name the inflammatory alternatives, because your tests must exclude them.

steps.label: Differential diagnosis
steps.info: The chest is clear, there are no skin nodules, no patches of whitened skin or lashes, and he has had no tinnitus or neck stiffness.
steps.q: List 4 differential diagnoses in rank order, each with one discriminating feature.
steps.key: 1. Ocular syphilis (early neurosyphilis) — painless disc swelling with uveitis after a chancre and palm–sole rash; reactive RPR and treponemal test. 2. Sarcoid-related optic neuropathy and uveitis — granulomatous uveitis, hilar lymph nodes, raised ACE; non-reactive treponemal test. 3. Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease — bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with serous retinal detachments, headache, tinnitus, later poliosis or vitiligo; no syphilitic rash. 4. Tuberculous or Lyme-related ocular inflammation — TB: chest findings and positive IGRA; Lyme: tick exposure in endemic regions (not Thailand) and confirmed only by two-tier testing. Bilateral papilloedema from raised pressure is unlikely: central vision is kept early and there is no uveitis.
steps.short: 1 ocular syphilis; 2 sarcoid; 3 VKH; 4 TB/Lyme; papilloedema unlikely.
steps.why: Each alternative earns its place by sharing 'disc swelling plus uveitis', and each has its own fingerprint: hilar nodes for sarcoid, serous detachments and hearing symptoms for VKH, chest disease for TB. Lyme is on the list mainly because its screening test can cross-react with syphilis, as you will see in the results.

steps.label: Investigations (tertiary centre)
steps.info: He is referred to a tertiary neurology institute in Bangkok with on-site ophthalmology, MRI and a full microbiology laboratory.
steps.q: What investigations would you order at a tertiary centre, and why?
tests: MRI brain and orbits with contrast
Lyme two-tier serology (ELISA then Western blot)
steps.key: Serum non-treponemal test with titre (RPR) plus a treponemal test (TPHA/TPPA or EIA): together they confirm syphilis, and the titre is the baseline for follow-up. HIV test, because coinfection is common and changes CSF interpretation and follow-up. LP with cells, protein, glucose, CSF VDRL (specific but insensitive) and a CSF treponemal test (sensitive; a negative result makes neurosyphilis unlikely) to document CNS involvement and give a baseline, although treatment of ocular syphilis does not depend on it. MRI brain and orbits with contrast for nerve-head or sheath enhancement, meningeal disease or a mass. Ophthalmology: slit lamp, dilated fundus, OCT, and fluorescein angiography if needed. Exclude mimics with chest X-ray and serum ACE (sarcoid) and IGRA (TB). Any Lyme screen must be confirmed by Western blot, because treponemal antibodies cross-react.
steps.short: RPR titre + TPHA; HIV; LP with CSF VDRL and CSF treponemal test; MRI orbits/brain with contrast; OCT ± FA; CXR, ACE, IGRA; Lyme only by two-tier testing.

kw: เจาะน้ำไขสันหลัง

steps.why: Pair a non-treponemal with a treponemal test: one tracks activity, the other confirms exposure. Do the LP to document nervous-system involvement and to have a baseline, but remember that ocular syphilis is treated as neurosyphilis even when the CSF is normal. And test for HIV every time you diagnose syphilis.

steps.label: Investigations (limited-resource hospital)
steps.info: Imagine he had presented to a community hospital: VDRL/RPR, TPHA, anti-HIV, CBC, chest X-ray, CT and basic CSF tests are available; there is no ophthalmologist and no MRI, and CSF VDRL must be sent to the provincial laboratory.
steps.q: What would you do there, what would you send out, and how can you still reach the diagnosis?
steps.key: Examine acuity, pupils and fundi with a direct ophthalmoscope: disc swelling and haemorrhages are visible, and a pen torch may show a hazy anterior chamber. Send RPR with titre and TPHA, which are routine in Thai hospitals, plus anti-HIV, CBC and chest X-ray. If there is headache, reduced consciousness or a focal sign, do CT before LP. Basic CSF (cells, protein, glucose) can be done locally; send CSF VDRL to the provincial laboratory. A high-titre reactive RPR with a reactive TPHA in a patient with uveitis and disc swelling is enough to diagnose ocular syphilis and start IV penicillin, or to refer the same day to a hospital that can give 10–14 days of it; arrange urgent ophthalmology review for slit-lamp confirmation.
steps.short: Fundoscopy; RPR titre + TPHA, anti-HIV, CXR; CT before LP if indicated; basic CSF, send CSF VDRL; positive serology + eye signs → start IV penicillin, refer to eye service.

points.c: Start treatment or refer without delay
kw: เพนิซิลลิน

steps.why: This is one of the most reachable diagnoses in a small hospital, because the decisive tests are cheap and routine. The danger is delay, not lack of technology: once serology is positive with eye inflammation, every day without penicillin risks permanent visual loss.

steps.label: Results and final diagnosis
steps.info: RPR reactive at 1:1024; TPHA reactive. A Lyme ELISA sent by the referring team is positive, but the Lyme Western blot is negative. Anti-HIV negative. CSF: 9 white cells/µL, all lymphocytes; protein 0.40 g/L; normal glucose; CSF VDRL non-reactive. MRI: enhancement of both optic nerve heads, with no meningeal enhancement or mass. Chest X-ray and serum ACE normal.
steps.q: What is the final diagnosis, how do you interpret the Lyme result and the negative CSF VDRL, and what is the mechanism in one line?
steps.key: Ocular syphilis (bilateral optic neuropathy with anterior uveitis and retinal involvement) in secondary syphilis, to be managed as neurosyphilis. The very high RPR with a reactive treponemal test confirms active infection. The positive Lyme ELISA with a negative Western blot is a false-positive screen from cross-reacting treponemal antibodies, not Lyme disease, and he has no exposure. A non-reactive CSF VDRL does not exclude neurosyphilis because the test is insensitive, and the mild lymphocytic pleocytosis supports CNS involvement. Mechanism: blood-borne Treponema pallidum inflames the uvea, retina and optic nerve head and its sheath.
steps.short: Ocular syphilis (= neurosyphilis) in secondary syphilis; Lyme ELISA false positive (blot negative); CSF VDRL insensitive; treponemal invasion of eye and nerve.

kw: ซิฟิลิสขึ้นตา

points.c: Treat as neurosyphilis regardless of CSF

steps.why: Two traps sit in these results. The Lyme screen is positive because syphilis antibodies cross-react, and the confirmatory blot is what counts. The CSF VDRL is negative, yet that test misses many true cases, so trust the whole picture and remember that eye involvement alone earns neurosyphilis treatment.

steps.label: Specific treatment
steps.info: He has no history of penicillin allergy, and the hospital can give IV infusions on the ward.
steps.q: What specific treatment would you give? Answer according to the CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (the Thai Department of Disease Control STI guideline uses the same first-line regimen).
steps.basis: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021 (neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis); the Thai Department of Disease Control national STI guideline is believed to be concordant — edition and wording to verify.
steps.key: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units per day IV, as 3–4 million units every 4 hours or as a continuous infusion, for 10–14 days. If IV therapy is not feasible and adherence is assured: procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once daily plus probenecid 500 mg orally four times daily, for 10–14 days. With penicillin allergy, ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily for 10–14 days may be used, or desensitise (required in pregnancy). Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM weekly for up to 3 weeks may be considered after the IV course. Steroids (topical, or systemic under ophthalmology) are adjuncts for uveitis only once penicillin has started.
steps.short: IV aqueous penicillin G 18–24 MU/day (3–4 MU q4h) × 10–14 days; alternatives procaine PCN + probenecid or ceftriaxone; steroids only as adjunct.

kw: เพนิซิลลิน
สเตียรอยด์เสริม

steps.why: Ocular syphilis gets the neurosyphilis regimen because benzathine penicillin does not reach adequate levels in the eye and CSF. Learn the numbers: 18 to 24 million units a day, every four hours, for ten to fourteen days. Steroids can calm the uveitis, but only behind the shield of penicillin.

steps.label: Supportive treatment and complications to monitor
steps.info: Six hours after the first dose of penicillin he develops a fever of 38.6 °C, aching muscles and a slight further blur in the right eye.
steps.q: What is happening, what supportive care would you give, and which complications would you monitor?
steps.key: A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (cytokine release from dying treponemes), usually within 24 hours: continue penicillin, give paracetamol and fluids and reassure; ophthalmology may add steroids if the eye inflammation flares. Supportive: topical steroid and cycloplegic drops for the anterior uveitis as directed by ophthalmology, IV line care. Monitor: acuity, fields and fundi for recovery or optic atrophy; intraocular pressure (uveitis, steroid drops); cystoid macular oedema; new meningitis, cranial nerve palsies or hearing loss (otosyphilis); and the serological response — the RPR should fall at least fourfold within 6–12 months. Repeat the CSF examination if it was abnormal and serology fails to fall or symptoms persist.
steps.short: Jarisch–Herxheimer: continue penicillin, antipyretic; topical steroid/cycloplegic; monitor vision, IOP, macular oedema, hearing, ≥4-fold RPR fall.
steps.why: Fever and slight worsening on the first day of penicillin is usually the Herxheimer reaction, not treatment failure or allergy, and stopping the drug would be the real mistake. Long-term success is measured by the fall in RPR titre, so record the baseline of 1:1024 carefully.

steps.label: Counselling
steps.info: By day 10 of penicillin acuity is 6/12 right and 6/9 left. He asks what this means for his partners.
steps.q: How would you counsel him, and what about his partners?
steps.key: Explain that syphilis has reached his eyes and is curable with penicillin; vision often improves a great deal if treated early, but some damage may remain. Contagion: he is infectious through sexual contact at this stage, so avoid sex until treatment is complete and lesions have healed. Partner notification: test all partners from at least the past 6 months plus the duration of his symptoms, and treat presumptively anyone exposed within the last 90 days. Repeat HIV testing after the window period, test for hepatitis B and C, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, offer HIV PrEP if he stays at risk, and advise condoms. Warning signs: new visual loss, eye pain, headache, hearing loss or weakness. Follow-up: serum RPR at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months and eye review. Treatment gives no lasting immunity, so reinfection is possible. Do not drive until acuity meets the standard. Any partner who is or may be pregnant needs urgent testing because of congenital syphilis.
steps.short: Curable; abstain until treated; notify partners (6 months + symptom duration), presumptive treatment for recent ones; HIV/STI tests, PrEP; RPR 3/6/12/24 months; reinfection possible; pregnant partners tested urgently.

kw: งดเพศสัมพันธ์

steps.why: Good syphilis care treats a community, not one patient. Partner notification, HIV testing and a plan for serological follow-up are as much part of treatment as the penicillin. Say clearly that cure gives no immunity, so protection still matters afterwards.

meq.title: A young technician who keeps blacking out

src.label: Chumbley et al., Neurology 2025 — Resident & Fellow Clinical Reasoning

compare: Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (Panayiotopoulos syndrome)
meq.stem: A 27-year-old man who maintains machines at an electronics factory in Ayutthaya is brought to the emergency room of the provincial hospital after collapsing at work. Coworkers say he turned pale, stopped talking mid-sentence, slid to the floor and was unresponsive for less than a minute, with a few jerks of both arms. He woke tired and a little muddled for about ten minutes. He says this is his fourth such episode in eight months, and two of them happened while he was sitting. He did not bite his tongue. He takes no medicines and drinks alcohol only at weekends.

steps.label: Initial approach
steps.q: What are the key questions and examinations, and what is your problem list?
steps.key: Decide between syncope, epileptic seizure and a functional event, and exclude danger first. From an eyewitness: posture and trigger (standing, heat, pain, exertion, lying down), warning symptoms (light-headedness, sweating, nausea versus a rising stomach feeling, déjà vu or a smell), colour change, duration, type of movements, eyes open or closed, automatisms, incontinence, and time to full recovery. Ask whether the attacks are identical each time and about any other sensations, including ones patients find embarrassing (genital sensations or erection); palpitations or chest pain before events, attacks during exercise, family history of sudden death or epilepsy, drugs, sleep loss, alcohol. Examine lying and standing BP, heart rate and rhythm, murmurs, injuries and a full neurological examination; do a 12-lead ECG and glucose now. Problem list: recurrent transient loss of consciousness with mixed syncopal and seizure-like features and brief post-event confusion.
steps.short: Eyewitness account; trigger, warning, movements, recovery; stereotypy and unusual sensations; cardiac red flags, ECG, orthostatic BP; problem = recurrent TLOC with mixed features.
