อาการเตือน
คลื่นไฟฟ้าหัวใจ
ความดันท่ายืน
เหมือนเดิมทุกครั้ง
เหมือนกันทุกครั้ง

steps.why: Transient loss of consciousness has three main doors — syncope, epilepsy and functional events — and a witness account opens the right one. Always clear the cardiac door first with an ECG and questions about exertion and family sudden death, because that door can kill. Then ask broadly about anything else that happens every time; patients often keep embarrassing symptoms to themselves.

steps.label: Localization
steps.info: Asked privately, he says each episode starts with a strange rising feeling in his stomach and a sense that the moment has happened before; then his heart seems to slow and his vision greys out. In the minute before every episode he notices an erection on only one side of the penis, which embarrasses him. A coworker who saw the last event says he smacked his lips and fumbled with his shirt for some seconds before turning pale. Examination between events is normal, and lying and standing BP shows no drop.
steps.q: Where does this process arise? Explain your reasoning.
steps.key: The cerebral cortex of the temporal lobe — the mesial temporal and limbic–insular network — probably on one side, to be lateralised by EEG. A rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu are classic mesial temporal auras, and lip-smacking and fumbling are oral and manual automatisms of a focal impaired-awareness seizure. The slowing heart and greying out mean an autonomic seizure: spread to the insula, amygdala and limbic autonomic network can cause ictal bradycardia or asystole and hypotension, so the seizure itself produces syncope. A stereotyped one-sided penile tumescence is a rare autonomic sign from the same network and may have localising value. Reflex syncope is unlikely: the aura and automatisms come before the pallor, events occur sitting, and there is post-event confusion.
steps.short: Temporal lobe (mesial / limbic–insular): epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms; autonomic spread → ictal bradycardia and syncope; unilateral tumescence = limbic autonomic sign.

kw: จุกลิ้นปี่
หัวใจเต้นช้า

steps.why: The order of events is your localiser: the aura and automatisms come first and the pallor second, so the brain starts the attack and the heart follows. Unusual autonomic signs such as a one-sided genital change are rarely volunteered, but when they appear in every attack they belong to the seizure, not to coincidence.

steps.label: Tempo, pattern and etiological category
steps.info: Further history: no febrile seizures in childhood, no head injury or meningitis, no relative with epilepsy or sudden death; memory and mood are normal.
steps.q: Describe the tempo and pattern, and the etiological category.
steps.key: Paroxysmal, recurrent, stereotyped episodes lasting about a minute, with full recovery between them, over 8 months: the pattern of epilepsy (epileptic category) — here focal impaired-awareness seizures with prominent cardiac autonomic features producing syncope. Then look for the cause of new focal epilepsy in a young adult: hippocampal sclerosis, a low-grade tumour (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, focal cortical dysplasia, damage from earlier infection or trauma, or autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. LGI1, uncommon at this age). The main alternative category is cardiac (arrhythmic) syncope, which can also produce brief jerks.
steps.short: Paroxysmal stereotyped episodes → epileptic (focal autonomic seizures causing syncope); search for a structural or autoimmune cause; exclude cardiac syncope.

kw: เป็นครั้งคราว

steps.why: Stereotypy is the hallmark of epilepsy: the same film plays every time. But a seizure that slows the heart produces syncope, so think of both systems together rather than choosing one. Once you accept focal epilepsy, the next question is always why this young brain has a focus.

steps.label: Differential diagnosis
steps.info: A cousin calls them fainting spells from overwork, and his manager wonders whether he is putting them on.
steps.q: Give a ranked differential diagnosis of 4 conditions, each with a discriminating feature.
steps.key: 1. Temporal lobe (focal) epilepsy with autonomic seizures causing ictal bradycardia and syncope — a stereotyped aura and automatisms precede the pallor; focal EEG changes. 2. Reflex (vasovagal) syncope — a clear trigger such as standing, heat or pain, a sweaty nauseated warning, and quick recovery without confusion; no aura or automatisms. 3. Cardiac arrhythmic syncope (long QT, Brugada, AV block, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) — onset on exertion or lying down, palpitations, family sudden death, abnormal ECG. 4. Functional (dissociative) seizures — long events with eyes closed, waxing and waning, side-to-side movements, emotional triggers, no autonomic change. Also consider hypoglycaemia.
steps.short: 1 TLE with ictal syncope; 2 reflex syncope; 3 cardiac arrhythmia; 4 functional seizures.

kw: ลมชักกลีบขมับ
หัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ

steps.why: Two diagnoses can be true at once here: the brain causes the seizure and the seizure makes the heart pause. Keep cardiac arrhythmia high on the list until the ECG and rhythm monitoring clear it, because missing it is the most dangerous error.

steps.label: Investigations (tertiary centre)
steps.info: He is referred to a tertiary neurology institute in Bangkok with an epilepsy monitoring unit.
steps.q: What investigations would you order at a tertiary centre, and why?
tests: Holter monitor or implantable loop recorder
steps.key: 12-lead ECG (QT interval, Brugada pattern, conduction block, pre-excitation). Routine and sleep-deprived EEG for temporal slowing or spikes. Video-EEG monitoring with a simultaneous ECG channel is the key test: a captured event shows the seizure onset and whether bradycardia or asystole follows it. MRI brain with an epilepsy protocol (thin coronal T2/FLAIR) for hippocampal sclerosis, tumour, cavernoma or dysplasia. Cardiac evaluation with echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring (Holter or an implantable loop recorder) when events are infrequent or an arrhythmia is still possible. Electrolytes, glucose, calcium and magnesium. If MRI shows limbic signal change or there are memory or psychiatric features, send autoimmune encephalitis antibodies (LGI1, CASPR2, NMDAR, GAD65).
steps.short: ECG; routine/sleep-deprived EEG; video-EEG with ECG channel; MRI epilepsy protocol; echo + Holter/loop recorder; electrolytes/glucose; autoimmune antibodies if indicated.

kw: คลื่นไฟฟ้าหัวใจ
คลื่นไฟฟ้าสมอง
เอ็มอาร์ไอ

steps.why: The most informative single test is an event captured on video-EEG with the ECG running, because it shows which came first — the electrical seizure or the heart pause. MRI then asks why. Cardiac tests are not a detour; they guard against the one diagnosis you cannot afford to miss.

steps.label: Investigations (limited-resource hospital)
steps.info: Suppose he had stayed at a community hospital: ECG and CT are available, routine EEG is offered once a week at the provincial hospital, and there is no MRI, video-EEG or Holter.
steps.q: What would you do there, what would you refer for, and how can you still reach a working diagnosis?
steps.key: Repeat the 12-lead ECG and lying and standing BP, and keep him on a cardiac monitor while admitted; check glucose and electrolytes. CT brain (with contrast if available) to exclude a large lesion, tumour or old injury, accepting that it misses hippocampal sclerosis and small lesions. Book a routine EEG at the provincial hospital, sleep-deprived if possible. Ask family and coworkers to film any event on a smartphone and to feel his pulse during it. Focal epilepsy can be diagnosed clinically from the stereotyped aura, automatisms and post-event confusion; start an antiseizure drug if the ECG is normal, and refer electively for MRI with an epilepsy protocol, video-EEG and prolonged ECG monitoring. Refer urgently if the ECG is abnormal, events occur on exertion, or there is a family history of sudden death.
steps.short: ECG, orthostatic BP, ward monitor, glucose/electrolytes, CT; routine EEG at provincial hospital; phone video + pulse; clinical diagnosis → start ASM; refer for MRI/VEEG/Holter.

kw: คลื่นไฟฟ้าหัวใจ
คลื่นไฟฟ้าสมอง
ถ่ายวิดีโอ

points.c: Clinical diagnosis, start ASM, refer for MRI
kw: เริ่มยากันชัก

steps.why: Epilepsy is a clinical diagnosis; tests support it but rarely make it alone. A phone video with someone feeling the pulse can be worth more than a normal routine EEG. At this level your main job is to make sure the heart is safe, then start treatment and send him for the tests that look for a cause.

steps.label: Results and final diagnosis
steps.info: 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram and a 48-hour Holter (no events recorded) are normal. Routine EEG: intermittent focal slowing over the left temporal region; no epileptiform discharges recorded. MRI brain with epilepsy protocol: no lesion seen. Electrolytes and glucose normal.
steps.q: What is the final diagnosis, and the mechanism in one line?
steps.key: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (temporal lobe epilepsy, MRI-negative so far) with focal impaired-awareness autonomic seizures that cause syncope (ictal syncope), together with stereotyped peri-ictal unilateral penile tumescence (hemidystumescence). Mechanism: the seizure discharge spreads into the limbic–insular autonomic network, altering heart rate and vascular tone (ictal bradycardia or hypotension) and genital autonomic control, which produces the loss of consciousness and the unusual genital sign. Normal cardiac tests make a primary arrhythmia unlikely, and the EEG supports a left temporal focus.
steps.short: Left TLE with autonomic seizures → ictal syncope + peri-ictal hemidystumescence; spread into the limbic–insular autonomic network.

kw: ลมชักกลีบขมับ
ลมชักเฉพาะที่

points.c: Peri-ictal genital sign belongs to the seizure

steps.why: A normal routine EEG and MRI would not have excluded epilepsy, but here the focal slowing gives you a side. Name both layers of the diagnosis — the epilepsy and the syncope it causes — because each has its own treatment and safety advice. The genital sign is a gift of localisation, not a separate disease.

steps.label: Specific treatment
steps.info: The team agrees on a working diagnosis of focal epilepsy and plans to start a drug. He weighs 68 kg and has no other illnesses.
steps.q: What antiseizure treatment would you start? Answer according to Thai practice (Epilepsy Society of Thailand clinical practice guideline), noting where it agrees with NICE NG217 (2022).
steps.basis: Epilepsy Society of Thailand clinical practice guideline for epilepsy (edition to verify); NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults (2022); Thai practice of HLA-B*15:02 screening before carbamazepine (verify current national recommendation).
steps.key: Start monotherapy with a drug for focal seizures: levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, titrated to 1000–1500 mg twice daily; or lamotrigine, titrated slowly from 25 mg daily over 6–8 weeks to 100–200 mg/day; or carbamazepine 100–200 mg twice daily titrated to 400–600 mg twice daily (controlled-release preferred). In Thai patients test HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine (and consider it before oxcarbazepine or phenytoin) because of the risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN. Choose by availability, cost, side effects and interactions, and prefer drugs without conduction effects if any heart conduction problem is suspected (carbamazepine, lacosamide and phenytoin can slow conduction). If ictal asystole is documented and seizures continue despite treatment, cardiology may consider a pacemaker to prevent falls and injury.
steps.short: Focal ASM monotherapy: levetiracetam / lamotrigine / carbamazepine (HLA-B*15:02 first); watch conduction effects; pacemaker only for documented refractory ictal asystole.

kw: เครื่องกระตุ้นหัวใจ

steps.why: Treating the seizure treats the syncope, because the heart was only following the brain. In Thailand, HLA-B*15:02 screening before carbamazepine is part of safe prescribing, not an extra. Choose one drug, give it properly, and judge it by whether the attacks — including the genital sign — stop.

steps.label: Supportive treatment and complications to monitor
steps.info: He starts levetiracetam. Over the next three months both the blackouts and the one-sided genital episodes stop.
steps.q: What supportive measures would you advise, and which complications would you monitor?
steps.key: Monitor: a seizure diary that includes the autonomic and genital symptoms as markers; drug adverse effects — irritability, low mood and suicidal thoughts with levetiracetam, rash with lamotrigine or carbamazepine, hyponatraemia and dizziness with carbamazepine; injuries from falls; drug resistance (failure of two appropriate, tolerated drugs means referral for epilepsy-surgery evaluation); SUDEP risk, highest with uncontrolled convulsive seizures; depression and anxiety, which are common in TLE; memory complaints. Supportive: regular sleep, limited alcohol, adherence, work safety (no heights or unguarded moving machinery until seizure-free), and first-aid training for coworkers. Repeat MRI if seizures recur or new signs appear.
steps.short: Seizure diary; drug side effects (mood on LEV, rash/Na on CBZ); injury, drug resistance → surgical work-up, SUDEP, mood; sleep, alcohol, work safety.

kw: ผลข้างเคียง

steps.why: Freedom from attacks is the goal, but you also watch the drug and the person. Levetiracetam can sour mood, and young men rarely report it unless asked. If two good drugs fail, refer for surgical evaluation early rather than adding drug after drug.

steps.label: Counselling
steps.info: He asks when he can ride his motorcycle to work again and whether he has to tell his employer.
steps.q: How would you counsel him and his family?
steps.key: Explain that the blackouts were caused by small seizures from the left temporal lobe that slowed his heart, not by heart disease, and that the one-sided erection was part of the seizure, not a sexual or urological disorder. The chance of seizure freedom on medication is good; take it every day and never stop suddenly. Driving: no driving until seizure-free for the period required by Thai licensing rules (12 months is common internationally). Work: avoid heights, ladders, unguarded machinery and working alone until controlled; involve occupational health. Emergency: a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery, needs an ambulance; also report rash or mood change on the drug. First aid for family and coworkers: lay him on his side, put nothing in the mouth, time the event, film it. Antiseizure drugs can affect sexual function, so report any problem. Genetics: usually not inherited; if relatives turn out to have similar epilepsy, discuss familial focal epilepsy and genetic counselling. Follow-up with EEG, and MRI as needed.
steps.short: Seizures caused the syncope; genital sign is part of the seizure; adherence; no driving until seizure-free per Thai rules; work safety; status warning; first aid; sexual side effects; genetics only if family history.

points.c: Explain diagnosis including the genital sign

ห้ามหยุดยา
เครื่องจักร

steps.why: He has carried an embarrassing symptom alone for months, and naming it as part of the seizure lifts a real burden. Be precise and practical about driving and work, because those are the decisions he will make the day he leaves. Give the family a simple first-aid script and a clear reason to call for help.

meq.monk: A young man has recurrent blackouts with both syncopal and seizure-like features. A careful private history uncovers the same sequence each time — a rising stomach feeling and déjà vu, lip-smacking and fumbling, then pallor and a slowing heart — and a one-sided penile erection before every attack. The aura and automatisms localise to the temporal lobe; the slowing heart and genital change reflect spread into the limbic–insular autonomic network, so the seizure causes the syncope. Cardiac arrhythmia is excluded with ECG, echocardiography and rhythm monitoring, and EEG shows left temporal slowing. The diagnosis is left temporal lobe epilepsy with autonomic seizures causing ictal syncope. A focal antiseizure drug, with HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine in Thai patients, stops both the blackouts and the genital sign; counselling covers adherence, driving, work safety and first aid.

meq.title: Fever, headache and a puffy left eye

src.label: Rexiati et al., Neurology 2026 — Resident & Fellow Clinical Reasoning

meq.stem: A 52-year-old woman who taps rubber trees in Nakhon Si Thammarat comes to the emergency room of a provincial hospital. For about a month the gum above her upper left back teeth has kept swelling and aching, and she has treated it with painkillers bought from a pharmacy. Four days ago she developed fever and a severe headache. Two days ago she began to see double when looking to the left, and since yesterday the skin around her left eye has become more and more puffy. She has hypertension, no known diabetes and no recent injury.

steps.label: Initial approach
steps.q: What would you ask and examine first, and what is your problem list?
steps.key: Judge severity first: vital signs, sepsis criteria, GCS and neck stiffness. Eyes: acuity, pupils and RAPD (optic nerve compression), eye movements tested for each of III, IV and VI, ptosis, proptosis, chemosis, lid swelling, pain on movement, corneal reflex and V1/V2 sensation, fundi (venous congestion, disc swelling), and the other eye for spread. Source: dental examination (abscess, tender tooth), sinuses, facial skin in the 'danger triangle', ears. History: diabetes, immunosuppression, recent dental work, antibiotics already taken. Check capillary glucose. Problem list: (1) fever with severe headache; (2) painful unilateral ophthalmoplegia with periorbital swelling; (3) a month of dental infection.
steps.short: Sepsis/vitals/GCS; III, IV, VI, V1/V2; acuity, RAPD, chemosis, proptosis, other eye; dental/sinus/face source; glucose; problem = febrile painful ophthalmoplegia + dental infection.

kw: ติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด

points.c: Cranial nerves III, IV, VI, V1/V2
kw: เส้นประสาทสมอง
เยื่อบุตาบวม

steps.why: Fever with a new eye-movement problem is an emergency until proven otherwise, so measure how sick she is before anything else. Then examine every nerve that runs through the cavernous sinus, because a pattern of III, IV, VI and the upper branches of V tells you where the trouble sits. A month of gum infection is not a side detail — it is the likely source.

steps.label: Localization
steps.info: T 38.9 °C, pulse 112/min, BP 108/70, GCS 15, no neck stiffness. Left eye: lid swelling, chemosis and mild proptosis; abduction is markedly limited and other movements are full; pupils equal and reactive with no RAPD; acuity 6/9 in both eyes; light touch reduced over the left forehead. The right eye is normal. The gum above the left upper molars is swollen and tender, with pus draining from a small sinus.
steps.q: Where is the lesion? Explain.
steps.key: The left cavernous sinus. A left abducens (VI) palsy with V1 sensory loss localises there: VI runs free in the sinus beside the internal carotid artery, and V1 runs in its lateral wall. Orbital congestion (chemosis, lid oedema, proptosis) shows obstructed venous outflow from the orbit through the superior ophthalmic vein into the sinus. Normal acuity and no RAPD argue against an orbital apex lesion involving the optic nerve, and simple orbital cellulitis usually limits all movements without V1 loss. A brainstem VI nucleus or fascicle lesion would bring a gaze palsy or long-tract signs, which are absent.
steps.short: Left cavernous sinus: VI palsy + V1 loss + orbital venous congestion; optic nerve spared → not orbital apex; no brainstem signs.

kw: คาเวอร์นัส
เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6

points.c: Venous congestion via superior ophthalmic vein
kw: เลือดดำคั่ง

steps.why: The abducens nerve floats in the middle of the cavernous sinus next to the carotid, so it is often the first nerve to fail there. Swelling and chemosis tell you the venous outflow from the orbit is blocked, pointing to the sinus that drains it. Sparing of vision places the lesion behind the orbit but in front of the brainstem.

steps.label: Tempo, pattern and etiological category
steps.info: She has had no facial injury, nasal discharge or black nasal crusts; the palate looks healthy and capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
steps.q: Describe the tempo and pattern, and name the most likely etiological category.
steps.key: A month of local dental infection, then acute fever and headache over days, followed within 48 hours by cranial neuropathy and orbital congestion: a febrile, rapidly progressive, unilateral painful ophthalmoplegia. Category: infective — septic thrombophlebitis of the cavernous sinus spreading from a dental source through the valveless pterygoid plexus and facial veins, or through the maxillary sinus. The cavernous ICA is exposed to the same infection (infectious arteritis). Inflammatory (Tolosa–Hunt) and neoplastic causes are much less likely with fever and a clear source.
steps.short: Local infection → acute febrile progressive painful ophthalmoplegia → infective: septic CST via valveless veins, ICA at risk.

kw: หลอดเลือดดำ
หลอดเลือดแดง

steps.why: Fever is the hinge: a painful ophthalmoplegia without fever leads you toward inflammation or tumour, and with fever toward infection. The veins of the face and teeth have no valves, so a neglected tooth can drain its infection backwards into the cavernous sinus. Remember that the carotid artery runs through that same infected space.

steps.label: Differential diagnosis
steps.info: There is no orbital bruit, the conjunctival vessels are not corkscrew-shaped, the nasal mucosa looks normal, and the right eye is still unaffected.
steps.q: Give a ranked differential diagnosis of 4 diseases, each with one discriminating feature.
steps.key: 1. Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis — fever, dental or sinus source, chemosis, VI with or without III/IV/V1, tendency to spread to the other eye; filling defects in the sinus and a thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein on imaging. 2. Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis or subperiosteal abscess — fever and proptosis confined to one orbit, globally limited movement, no V1 loss, no sinus filling defect. 3. Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis — diabetes, ketoacidosis or immunosuppression, black eschar in the nose or palate, orbital apex syndrome with visual loss. 4. Carotid–cavernous fistula — chemosis and proptosis with arterialised conjunctival vessels and an orbital bruit, usually without fever. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome (painful ophthalmoplegia without fever, steroid-responsive) is a diagnosis of exclusion.
steps.short: 1 septic CST; 2 orbital cellulitis; 3 mucormycosis; 4 CCF; Tolosa–Hunt only by exclusion.

kw: เบ้าตาอักเสบ

steps.why: All four can swell an eye, but each leaves its own mark: a sinus filling defect, a confined orbit, a black eschar, or a bruit with corkscrew vessels. Mucormycosis must be actively excluded in anyone with diabetes because its treatment is very different. Tolosa–Hunt is a diagnosis you earn only after infection is excluded.

steps.label: Investigations (tertiary centre)
steps.info: She is transferred to a tertiary centre with MRI, CT angiography, catheter angiography and maxillofacial surgery.
steps.q: What investigations would you order at a tertiary centre, and why?
tests: Contrast MRI brain and orbits with MR venography
steps.key: Two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, without delaying antibiotics for imaging. CBC, CRP, renal function, glucose and HbA1c, and HIV if indicated. Contrast MRI of brain and orbits with MR venography (or contrast CT with CT venography): an enlarged cavernous sinus with filling defects, a dilated thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein, orbital spread, meningitis or abscess. Arterial imaging of the cavernous ICA with CTA or MRA, and catheter angiography (DSA) when abnormal, because infection can narrow the artery or later create an aneurysm. Source imaging: CT of sinuses and face and an orthopantomogram or dental CT; pus for Gram stain and aerobic, anaerobic and fungal culture. LP if meningitis is suspected and imaging shows no contraindication.
steps.short: Blood cultures before antibiotics; CBC/CRP/glucose; MRI + MRV (or CTV); CTA/MRA ± DSA of cavernous ICA; CT sinuses/face + OPG; pus culture; LP if meningitis.

kw: เพาะเชื้อในเลือด

points.c: MRI with MRV or CT venography
kw: เอ็มอาร์ไอ
ฉีดสีหลอดเลือด
เอกซเรย์ฟัน

steps.why: Venous imaging confirms the thrombosed sinus, but here the artery deserves equal attention because it runs through the infected sinus. Finding the source is part of both diagnosis and treatment: without draining the tooth, antibiotics fight with one hand tied. Cultures taken before the first dose are your only chance to know the organism.

steps.label: Investigations (limited-resource hospital)
steps.info: Suppose she had stayed at a district hospital: contrast CT is available at the provincial hospital 60 km away; routine blood tests and blood cultures can be sent; a dentist is on site; there is no MRI or angiography.
steps.q: What would you do there, what would you send out or refer for, and how can you still reach the diagnosis?
tests: Contrast CT of head, orbits and sinuses
steps.key: Recognise the clinical syndrome — fever, chemosis and proptosis, a VI palsy and a dental source — which is enough to act on. Take blood cultures and CBC, check glucose, then give the first IV antibiotic doses at once (ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, adding cloxacillin or vancomycin according to local resistance) with fluids for sepsis. The dentist examines, takes a dental X-ray and drains or extracts if safe. Refer urgently to the provincial or tertiary hospital for contrast CT of head, orbits and sinuses (with CT venography if possible), then MRI and vascular imaging, maxillofacial surgery, neurology and ophthalmology. LP only if meningitis is suspected, and after CT. Never delay antibiotics for imaging.
steps.short: Clinical diagnosis; blood cultures, CBC, glucose; first IV antibiotics now; dental X-ray ± drainage; urgent referral for contrast CT/CTV and specialists.

points.c: Clinical recognition is enough to act
Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics before transfer
kw: ยาปฏิชีวนะ
ยาฆ่าเชื้อ

points.c: Urgent referral for contrast CT / CTV

steps.why: In a small hospital the best test is your recognition of the pattern, and the most important treatment is the first antibiotic dose given before the ambulance leaves. A dentist on site is a real asset, because the source can sometimes be drained the same day. Imaging confirms; it should never delay.

steps.label: Results and final diagnosis
steps.info: Contrast MRI with MR venography: the left cavernous sinus is enlarged with non-enhancing filling defects, the left superior ophthalmic vein is dilated and thrombosed, and there is inflammation around the roots of the left upper molars and in the left maxillary sinus. CTA and then catheter angiography: the cavernous part of the left ICA is markedly narrowed. Panoramic X-ray: periapical abscess of the left upper second molar. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus anginosus group; dental pus also grows anaerobes. Glucose 6.2 mmol/L, HbA1c normal.
steps.q: What is the final diagnosis and its mechanism in one line, and what does the ICA finding imply?
steps.key: Left septic cavernous sinus thrombosis from an odontogenic (dental) infection, complicated by infectious arteritis with severe narrowing of the cavernous internal carotid artery. Mechanism: bacteria from the molar abscess travel backwards through valveless pterygoid and facial veins into the cavernous sinus, causing septic thrombophlebitis that compresses the cranial nerves, blocks orbital venous drainage and inflames the neighbouring ICA wall. The ICA involvement carries a risk of ischaemic stroke now and of a new aneurysmal lesion later at the same site (typically an infectious, mycotic pseudoaneurysm), so interval vascular imaging is required.
steps.short: Left septic CST from a dental abscess, with infectious arteritis of the cavernous ICA → stroke risk now, aneurysm risk later.

steps.label: Emergency management
steps.info: While she waits for a bed her BP falls to 92/58 mmHg and lactate is 3.1 mmol/L.
steps.q: What is the emergency management in the first hours?
steps.basis: Surviving Sepsis Campaign international guidelines 2021 for initial sepsis care; antibiotic choice and source control follow standard textbook and review practice for septic cavernous sinus thrombosis (no dedicated guideline).
steps.key: Airway, breathing, circulation and sepsis resuscitation: IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg if hypotensive or lactate is high, vasopressors if needed. Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour at meningeal doses, covering streptococci, S. aureus (MRSA if at risk) and mouth anaerobes: vancomycin (loading 20–35 mg/kg, then by levels) or cloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours if MRSA is unlikely, plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours, plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. Urgent source control by the dental or maxillofacial team (drain the abscess, extract the tooth) and ENT drainage if the sinus is involved. Analgesia, antipyretics and eye care (lubrication if the lids cannot close). Neurological observations for meningitis, falling consciousness, stroke signs or spread to the other eye.
steps.short: Sepsis resuscitation; within 1 h IV vancomycin (or cloxacillin) + ceftriaxone 2 g q12h + metronidazole 500 mg q8h; urgent dental/sinus drainage; eye care; neuro obs.

steps.why: In the first hour you are treating sepsis that happens to sit behind the eye. Choose antibiotics that reach the CSF and cover mouth anaerobes, because the source is a tooth. Source control is not optional — a pocket of pus keeps seeding the sinus no matter how good the drugs are.

steps.label: Specific treatment
steps.info: The neurosurgery team asks whether to start anticoagulation; repeat imaging shows no intracranial haemorrhage.
steps.q: What specific treatment would you give beyond the first hours? (No Thai or international guideline is dedicated to septic cavernous sinus thrombosis; answer by standard textbook and review practice.)
steps.basis: Standard textbook and review-article practice for septic cavernous sinus thrombosis (no dedicated Thai or international guideline); evidence for anticoagulation is observational only.
steps.key: Continue IV antibiotics guided by culture — for S. anginosus with anaerobes, for example ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours (or high-dose IV penicillin G) plus metronidazole — for at least 3–4 weeks, often 4–6 weeks when the artery is involved or there is an abscess, then reassess with imaging. Complete source control (tooth extraction, sinus drainage). Anticoagulation: consider therapeutic LMWH or unfractionated heparin (e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 hours) once intracranial haemorrhage is excluded, to limit thrombus spread; the evidence is observational, so weigh it against the bleeding risk from the inflamed ICA and discuss with neurointervention. Corticosteroids only for documented pituitary insufficiency (hydrocortisone) or selected severe orbital inflammation once antibiotics are established.
steps.short: Culture-guided IV antibiotics ≥3–4 (often 4–6) weeks; complete source control; consider LMWH/UFH after haemorrhage excluded; steroids only for pituitary failure.

steps.label: Supportive treatment and complications to monitor
steps.info: Over two weeks the fever settles, the chemosis resolves and abduction improves. She is discharged to complete antibiotics.
steps.q: What supportive care would you give, and which complications would you monitor, including after discharge?
steps.key: Supportive: analgesia, eye lubrication and protection, patching or prisms for diplopia, nutrition, glucose control, IV line care and dental follow-up. Monitor in hospital: spread to the other cavernous sinus and eye, meningitis, brain abscess, ischaemic stroke from the narrowed ICA, visual loss (optic nerve or retinal vessel occlusion), sepsis, bleeding on anticoagulation, and antibiotic toxicity (vancomycin levels, renal function). After discharge: pituitary insufficiency (morning cortisol, sodium, thyroid tests), persisting cranial nerve palsy, and interval vascular imaging of the cavernous ICA (CTA or MRA, with DSA if abnormal — for example at 1–3 months, 6 months and 1 year) to detect a new aneurysmal lesion, typically an infectious pseudoaneurysm, which may need endovascular treatment.
steps.short: Eye care, diplopia patch; watch contralateral spread, meningitis, abscess, stroke, vision, bleeding, drug toxicity; later pituitary tests and scheduled CTA/MRA/DSA for a new aneurysm.

steps.why: Feeling better is not the end of this disease. The most dangerous late event — an aneurysm forming where the artery was inflamed — is silent until it bleeds or clots, so it must be looked for on a schedule. The pituitary sits next door too, and its failure can be quiet.

steps.label: Counselling
steps.info: At 3 months she is well, with only mild double vision on far left gaze.
steps.q: How would you counsel the patient and her family?
steps.key: Explain that an untreated tooth infection spread through facial veins to a vein channel behind the eye and inflamed the neighbouring brain artery; she has responded well, but the double vision may take weeks to months to recover and may not fully resolve. Most patients survive with treatment, though some keep nerve palsies or visual problems. She must finish the full antibiotic course and the dental treatment; regular dental check-ups and early treatment of tooth or sinus infection prevent recurrence. It is not contagious and not inherited. Return at once for new fever, severe headache, worsening vision or eye swelling, weakness or speech trouble, or a sudden severe headache or heavy nosebleed (possible aneurysm rupture). Keep every scheduled vascular scan even when well, plus pituitary tests and neurology and ophthalmology review. No driving while she has double vision; return to rubber tapping when diplopia and fatigue allow. On anticoagulants: bleeding precautions and no NSAIDs.
steps.short: Explain dental → venous → arterial spread; finish antibiotics and dental care; warning signs incl. sudden headache/nosebleed; keep scheduled vascular scans; no driving with diplopia.

steps.why: The family must understand why someone who looks cured still needs scans, or they will skip them. Give warning signs that match the late risks — a sudden severe headache or a nosebleed can signal an aneurysm of the cavernous carotid. End with prevention: the next tooth infection should be treated early.

meq.monk: A woman with a month of gum infection develops fever and headache, then double vision on looking left and a swollen, chemotic left eye. A left abducens palsy with V1 sensory loss and orbital venous congestion localises to the left cavernous sinus; fever and a dental source make the category infective, with spread through the valveless facial and pterygoid veins. Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis heads a differential of orbital cellulitis, mucormycosis and carotid–cavernous fistula. Imaging confirms sinus thrombosis with a thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein, and angiography shows severe narrowing of the cavernous ICA from infectious arteritis. Treatment is sepsis care, immediate broad IV antibiotics covering streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes for weeks, drainage of the dental source and considered anticoagulation. Because an inflamed artery can later form a new aneurysm at the same site, interval vascular imaging is scheduled even after full clinical recovery.

meq.title: A retired man who suddenly cannot find his words

src.label: Gutierrez-Albizuri et al., Neurology 2025 — Resident & Fellow Clinical Reasoning

meq.stem: A 66-year-old retired bus driver is brought by his daughter to the stroke fast-track of a tertiary neurology institute in Bangkok. He was well at breakfast, but by late morning he was muddled, could not follow the conversation and was producing jumbled sentences; she cannot say exactly when it started. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and drinks one or two glasses of beer at weekends. He does not report fever or headache. On arrival he is drowsy but rousable; BP 168/92, capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L, temperature 37.2 °C.

steps.label: Initial approach
steps.q: What do you do first, and what is your problem list?
steps.key: Treat as a possible acute stroke while screening for mimics: airway and breathing, last-known-well time, glucose (done), NIHSS, and urgent CT with CTA (or MRI) for reperfusion decisions. Separate true aphasia from confusion and inattention by testing naming, repetition, comprehension and fluency against fluctuating attention. Look for signs of a wider encephalopathy: asterixis, myoclonus, subtle twitching or eye deviation (non-convulsive seizures), meningism, fever, rash, stigmata of liver disease. Collateral history: new medicines, sedatives or supplements, alcohol, recent infection, urinary symptoms, fasting or high-protein meals, earlier similar episodes. Problem list: (1) acute confusional state (encephalopathy) with (2) a language disturbance; (3) uncertain onset time; (4) hypertension.
steps.short: Stroke pathway (LKW, NIHSS, CT/CTA) plus mimic screen; aphasia vs confusion; asterixis/myoclonus/subtle seizures; drug and diet history; problem = acute encephalopathy with language disturbance.

kw: หลอดเลือดสมอง

steps.why: Acute language trouble belongs on the stroke pathway until proven otherwise, because minutes matter there. Keep a second lens open, though: many patients called aphasic are actually confused, and confusion points to the whole brain rather than one artery. Asterixis or tiny rhythmic twitches hint that the problem is metabolic or epileptic.

steps.label: Localization
steps.info: NIHSS 6: drowsy, misses orientation questions, follows only one command, fluent speech full of paraphasic errors with poor comprehension; no limb weakness, no gaze deviation, no field defect detectable in this drowsy state. Attention fluctuates and there is bilateral asterixis. Non-contrast CT brain is normal and CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion. Onset time is unknown and he is outside the treatment window.
steps.q: Where is the dysfunction? Explain your reasoning.
steps.key: Diffuse, bilateral cerebral (cortical) dysfunction — an encephalopathy — with prominent involvement of the dominant hemisphere language network. Fluctuating attention, drowsiness and bilateral asterixis indicate a global process affecting both hemispheres and the arousal systems rather than one vascular territory. Fluent paraphasic speech with poor comprehension reflects posterior perisylvian (temporal) language cortex, which metabolic, epileptic or encephalitic processes can affect preferentially. No motor signs and a normal CTA make a single large-vessel stroke unlikely.
steps.short: Diffuse bilateral cortical dysfunction (encephalopathy) with dominant perisylvian language involvement; asterixis = global/metabolic; not one vascular territory.

steps.why: Aphasia sounds focal, but drowsiness, fluctuating attention and asterixis tell you the whole cortex is unwell. A diffuse insult can still be loudest in one function — here language — so do not let one prominent sign override the global picture. A negative CTA lowers the chance of a large-artery stroke.

steps.label: Tempo, pattern and etiological category
steps.info: Over the next 12 hours he has two seizures that begin with twitching of the right face and arm and become bilateral tonic–clonic. IV lorazepam 4 mg stops them, and the team gives an IV valproate load of 30 mg/kg and continues 500 mg twice daily. The next day he is drowsier than before (GCS 10, E3V2M5), has vomited twice and has frequent multifocal myoclonic jerks. His daughter adds that he has always disliked meat and eggs, and twice in the past 5 years he was confused for a day after large festive meals.
steps.q: Describe the tempo and pattern, and the etiological categories to consider.
steps.key: Acute (hours) encephalopathy with aphasia, then seizures, then deterioration after valproate: acute and progressive. Categories: (1) toxic–metabolic, above all hyperammonaemia — worse after valproate, with vomiting and myoclonus, and a history of protein aversion and confusion after protein-rich meals that suggests a hidden urea-cycle disorder; also hyponatraemia, uraemia, liver failure, hypercalcaemia, Wernicke's encephalopathy; (2) infective — HSV or other viral encephalitis; (3) inflammatory — autoimmune encephalitis; (4) epileptic — non-convulsive status epilepticus; (5) vascular — now less likely (multiple territories, PRES). Worsening after valproate is itself a red flag for valproate-associated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy.
steps.short: Acute encephalopathy + seizures, worse after valproate, protein-aversion history → metabolic (hyperammonaemia/UCD) vs viral or autoimmune encephalitis vs NCSE.

kw: สมองอักเสบ
ชักต่อเนื่อง

steps.why: When a patient gets worse after you start a drug, first ask whether the drug is part of the problem. Valproate can raise ammonia even at normal blood levels, and someone who has avoided protein all his life may carry a mild inherited defect in clearing it. Keep encephalitis and non-convulsive status on the list, because they are treatable too.

steps.label: Differential diagnosis
steps.info: Repeat sodium is 138 mmol/L, he remains afebrile, and there are no signs of chronic liver disease.
steps.q: Give a ranked differential diagnosis of 5 diseases, each with one discriminating feature.
steps.key: 1. Non-hepatic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy (valproate-associated, possibly with an underlying urea-cycle disorder) — worse after valproate, vomiting, asterixis or myoclonus, normal liver tests, high plasma ammonia; MRI shows insular and cingulate cortical oedema. 2. Herpes simplex encephalitis — fever, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, asymmetric mesial temporal, insular and cingulate lesions, positive HSV PCR. 3. Non-convulsive status epilepticus — fluctuating responsiveness with ongoing seizure activity on EEG that improves with a benzodiazepine. 4. Autoimmune (limbic) encephalitis — subacute memory and behaviour change, faciobrachial dystonic seizures or hyponatraemia (LGI1), positive neuronal antibodies. 5. Sporadic CJD — progression over weeks to months with myoclonus, cortical ribboning and basal ganglia DWI change, periodic sharp waves; unlikely with this acute onset. Also: Wernicke's, hepatic encephalopathy, PRES.
steps.short: 1 hyperammonaemic encephalopathy; 2 HSE; 3 NCSE; 4 autoimmune encephalitis; 5 sCJD.
steps.why: Rank by what kills or cures fastest. Hyperammonaemia and herpes encephalitis are both treatable and both can light up the insula and cingulate, so you need tests that split them quickly: ammonia and CSF PCR. Start acyclovir while you wait if encephalitis is a real possibility.

steps.label: Investigations (tertiary centre)
steps.info: He is admitted to the neuro-intensive care unit.
steps.q: What investigations would you order at a tertiary centre, and why?
tests: Electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and renal function
MRI brain with DWI and FLAIR
steps.key: Plasma ammonia now — free-flowing venous or arterial sample, on ice, analysed within 30 minutes — with liver function tests, INR, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function, glucose, blood gas and lactate, and a valproate level (ammonia can be high with a normal level). MRI brain with DWI and FLAIR: insular–cingulate cortical oedema (hyperammonaemia) versus mesial temporal lesions (HSE), cortical ribboning (CJD) or peri-ictal change. Continuous EEG for NCSE. LP with cells, protein, glucose and HSV/VZV PCR; consider autoimmune encephalitis antibodies. Search for the cause of hyperammonaemia: urinalysis and culture (urease-producing organisms with retention), abdominal ultrasound with Doppler for cirrhosis or a portosystemic shunt, a full drug review, and metabolic tests for a urea-cycle disorder — plasma amino acids (glutamine, citrulline, arginine) and urine orotic acid, followed by genetic testing.
steps.short: Ammonia on ice + LFT/INR, electrolytes, VPA level; MRI DWI/FLAIR; cEEG; LP with HSV PCR; urine culture, liver Doppler; plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid → genetics.

points.c: Urea-cycle tests: amino acids, orotic acid, genetics
Other causes: liver tests, VPA level, urine culture, shunt

steps.why: Ammonia is the cheapest test with the biggest yield here, but only if drawn properly — a warm or slow sample gives a falsely high value. Then ask the second question: why is ammonia high when the liver is normal? Drugs, urinary infection, shunts and inherited urea-cycle defects are the answers to search for.

steps.label: Investigations (limited-resource hospital)
steps.info: Imagine he had presented to a general hospital: CT, routine blood and liver tests, basic CSF and a weekday EEG are available; plasma ammonia is not measured in house; there is no MRI and no metabolic laboratory.
steps.q: What would you do there, what would you send out or refer for, and how can you still reach the diagnosis?
steps.key: Suspect hyperammonaemia clinically in anyone on valproate who becomes drowsier, vomits or develops asterixis, even with normal liver tests. Send a correctly handled ammonia sample on ice to the nearest laboratory that measures it, but do not wait for it: stop valproate and switch to another IV antiseizure drug (levetiracetam or phenytoin), stop protein intake, give IV dextrose and lactulose, and L-carnitine if available. Check liver tests, electrolytes, renal function, glucose and urinalysis. CT to exclude haemorrhage or a mass; LP for basic CSF; if the CSF is inflammatory or there is fever, start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours and send CSF for HSV PCR. Use EEG when available. Improvement after stopping valproate supports the diagnosis. Refer to a tertiary centre for MRI, ammonia monitoring, possible dialysis and metabolic testing (plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid, genetics).
steps.short: Clinical suspicion; send ammonia on ice; stop VPA and switch ASM; no protein, IV dextrose, lactulose ± carnitine; LFT/electrolytes/UA; CT + basic CSF; acyclovir if CSF inflamed; refer.

points.c: Clinical suspicion despite normal liver tests

kw: อะไซโคลเวียร์

steps.why: You do not need a machine to stop a drug that may be harming the patient. If valproate is a suspect, replacing it with another antiseizure drug costs little and can save a life. Keep acyclovir at hand whenever encephalitis is possible, and refer for the tests and dialysis a small hospital cannot provide.

steps.label: Results and final diagnosis
steps.info: Plasma ammonia 212 µmol/L (reference < 50); liver enzymes, bilirubin, albumin and INR normal; valproate level 78 mg/L (within range). Sodium, renal function and urinalysis normal. EEG: diffuse slowing of the background, no ongoing seizures. CSF: 1 cell/µL, protein 0.38 g/L, normal glucose; HSV PCR negative. MRI: bilateral, symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with restricted diffusion in the insular and cingulate cortex, relatively sparing the perirolandic cortex. Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler: normal liver, no portosystemic shunt.
steps.q: What is the final diagnosis, and what is the mechanism in one line?
steps.key: Non-hepatic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, precipitated or worsened by valproate, with a suspected underlying late-onset partial urea-cycle disorder (protein aversion, earlier post-meal episodes, encephalopathy before valproate) to be confirmed by plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and genetic testing. Mechanism: valproate, through propionyl-CoA and carnitine depletion, inhibits carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and the urea cycle; excess ammonia enters astrocytes and becomes glutamine, which draws in water and causes cytotoxic oedema, most visible in the insular and cingulate cortex. Normal liver tests and Doppler exclude hepatic and shunt causes; normal CSF and negative HSV PCR make encephalitis unlikely.
steps.short: Non-hepatic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy worsened by valproate, suspected underlying UCD; VPA inhibits CPS1 → astrocyte glutamine → insular/cingulate oedema.

kw: แอมโมเนียสูง

points.c: Normal liver tests exclude hepatic cause

steps.why: The MRI pattern — insula and cingulate on both sides — is the imaging fingerprint that pulls this case together. Valproate explains the deterioration, but the story before the drug and the lifelong dislike of protein invite a deeper question: is there an inherited weakness of the urea cycle? Put that question into the diagnosis, because the answer matters for him and his family.

steps.label: Emergency management
steps.info: While results return, his GCS drifts to 9 and he has another brief seizure; pupils are equal and reactive.
steps.q: What is the emergency management?
steps.basis: European guidelines for urea cycle disorders (Häberle et al., 2012; revision 2019) for ammonia thresholds, scavengers and dialysis; standard toxicology practice for L-carnitine in valproate hyperammonaemia; American Epilepsy Society 2016 guideline for seizure control.
steps.key: Airway: GCS 9 — protect the airway (intubate if GCS ≤ 8 or aspiration risk) and manage in ICU. Stop valproate at once and control seizures with another drug (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, maximum 4.5 g, as a load); avoid topiramate, which can also raise ammonia. Stop protein for 24–48 hours but prevent catabolism with high calories: IV 10% dextrose (insulin if hyperglycaemic) with or without IV lipid. Ammonia scavengers: IV sodium benzoate and/or sodium phenylacetate (loading about 250 mg/kg over 90–120 minutes, then 250 mg/kg/day, using surface-area dosing in adults per the guideline) with IV arginine (loading about 250 mg/kg). L-carnitine IV 100 mg/kg (maximum 6 g) as a load, then 15 mg/kg every 4 hours, for the valproate component. Urgent haemodialysis or CRRT if ammonia is above about 400–500 µmol/L, rising despite treatment, or with coma or cerebral oedema. Lactulose by nasogastric tube is often added. Treat raised ICP (head up 30°, osmotherapy) if present, and recheck ammonia every 3–4 hours.
steps.short: Airway/ICU; stop VPA, levetiracetam for seizures; no protein 24–48 h, IV dextrose; sodium benzoate/phenylacetate + arginine; L-carnitine; dialysis if NH3 >400–500 or coma; NH3 every 3–4 h.
steps.why: Two things lower ammonia fast: stopping what raises it and removing what is already there. Withdraw valproate, block protein breakdown with calories and give scavengers; if the level is very high or he is in coma, call for dialysis early, because brain swelling can follow quickly. Carnitine is the specific antidote for the valproate part of the problem.

steps.label: Specific treatment
steps.info: Ammonia falls to 48 µmol/L after 36 hours of scavengers and L-carnitine without dialysis; he wakes, and his speech improves over 5 days. Plasma amino acids and urine orotic acid have been sent to a reference laboratory.
steps.q: What specific (cause-directed) treatment would you plan?
steps.basis: European guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders (Häberle et al., 2012; revision 2019) for long-term care; review literature and standard practice for valproate-associated hyperammonaemia.
steps.key: Never restart valproate: record it as a serious adverse reaction and choose a long-term antiseizure drug without ammonia effects (levetiracetam or lamotrigine), avoiding topiramate as well. Treat the cause: if a urea-cycle disorder is confirmed, a metabolic specialist and dietitian set a protein-controlled diet with essential amino acid supplements, oral nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate or sodium/glycerol phenylbutyrate) and arginine or citrulline according to the defect, plus a written emergency (sick-day) regimen for illness, fasting, surgery or large protein loads. Avoid other triggers such as high-dose steroids, asparaginase and prolonged fasting. If metabolic tests are negative, record valproate-induced hyperammonaemia and correct contributing factors (carnitine deficiency, infection).
steps.short: Never re-use valproate; LEV/LTG long term; if UCD: protein-controlled diet + EAA, oral benzoate/phenylbutyrate, arginine/citrulline, sick-day plan; avoid triggers.

steps.why: The crisis is over, but the real treatment is preventing the next one. If an inherited urea-cycle defect is confirmed, a diet, a scavenger and a written emergency plan keep him safe through the next infection or feast. Whatever the result, valproate should never be given to him again.

steps.label: Supportive treatment and complications to monitor
steps.info: On day 3 he is awake on the ward but tired, with pauses to find words; potassium is 3.1 mmol/L.
steps.q: What supportive care would you give, and which complications would you monitor?
steps.key: Supportive: ICU nursing, aspiration precautions, early enteral feeding with controlled protein, glucose monitoring, DVT prophylaxis, speech and language therapy, early mobilisation and delirium care. Monitor: ammonia every 3–4 hours until stable, then daily; GCS and pupils for cerebral oedema and raised ICP; seizures (EEG if responsiveness fluctuates); electrolytes and acid–base — sodium benzoate and phenylacetate can cause hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis, and arginine hydrochloride a hyperchloraemic acidosis; the sodium and fluid load from scavengers; aspiration pneumonia; catabolism and nutrition; residual cognitive and language deficits; and repeat MRI to confirm resolution.
steps.short: ICU care, controlled-protein feeding, SLT, DVT prophylaxis; monitor NH3, GCS/ICP, seizures, K+/acid–base from scavengers, aspiration, nutrition, residual cognition.

steps.why: The scavengers carry a sodium load and can upset potassium and acid–base balance, so check electrolytes as often as ammonia. Brain swelling is the complication that kills, and it hides behind sedation unless you watch the pupils and the trend. Rehabilitation for language and thinking starts as soon as he can take part.

steps.label: Counselling
steps.info: Before discharge his daughter asks whether she or her children could have the same problem.
steps.q: How would you counsel the patient and his family?
steps.key: Explain that a toxic level of ammonia, raised by valproate and possibly by an inherited weakness in the body's ammonia-clearing (urea) cycle, caused the confusion and seizures; he has largely recovered, but some memory or language difficulty may persist and improve over months. Never take valproate again; carry a medical alert card or letter. Warning signs: drowsiness, confusion, vomiting or flapping hands, especially after illness, fasting, a big protein meal or a new drug — go to hospital and ask for an ammonia test. Genetic counselling is essential if a urea-cycle disorder is confirmed: most are autosomal recessive (each sibling has a 1 in 4 risk; his children are usually carriers), whereas OTC deficiency is X-linked (all his daughters would be carriers who can have symptoms, and their sons are at risk). Offer testing to blood relatives and preconception counselling to his daughters. Driving: not until seizure-free and cognitively assessed, per Thai rules. Follow-up: neurology, metabolic clinic, dietitian, EEG and repeat MRI.
steps.short: Explain ammonia cause; never valproate (alert card); warning signs after illness/fasting/protein; genetic counselling (AR vs X-linked OTC — daughters carriers) and family testing; no driving until seizure-free; follow-up.

steps.why: This counselling reaches beyond one man: if he carries a urea-cycle defect, his brothers, sisters and daughters need to know, because a first crisis can strike after childbirth, surgery or a fast. Give him a card to show any future doctor so valproate is never repeated, and tie the warning signs to triggers he can recognise.

meq.monk: An older man develops sudden confusion with fluent paraphasic speech; stroke imaging is negative, and drowsiness, fluctuating attention and asterixis reveal a diffuse encephalopathy rather than a single vascular lesion. Seizures follow and valproate is started, after which he worsens with vomiting and myoclonus — a red flag for drug-related hyperammonaemia. The differential includes herpes encephalitis, non-convulsive status, autoimmune encephalitis and CJD, which CSF PCR, EEG, antibodies and the MRI pattern separate. Normal CSF, diffuse EEG slowing, bilateral insular and cingulate cortical diffusion restriction, a high ammonia with normal liver tests and a history of protein aversion point to non-hepatic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy worsened by valproate, with a possible underlying urea-cycle disorder. Stop valproate, give calories without protein, scavengers, arginine and L-carnitine, dialyse if ammonia is very high, then confirm the metabolic cause and offer the family genetic counselling.
